speechtext: Explain.

maintopic: CANADIAN CITIZENSHIP ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT REMOVING WAITING PERIOD FOR PAPERS FOR LANDED RESIDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a small amendment but I think a very meaningful one. The purpose of this bill is to convey to new Canadians and to landed immigrants in a meaningful way the commemoration of our centennial. Under this bill every legally landed resident of Canada will be entitled to receive citizenship papers on or after July 1, 1967, our national birthday, without waiting for the five year period or any other qualification save and except taking the oath of allegiance. It may surprise hon. members to know that there are over a quarter of a million residents of Canada who are entitled to take out citizenship papers but who for one reason or another have not done so. I believe that if this bill is passed, or the government sees fit to pass legislation to this effect, many future citizens of Canada will have cause to remember our national birthday as the day on which they became citizens of Canada.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to legalize abortion, a practice that is very widespread in Canada and elsewhere. This bill seeks to end a situation where a law which cannot be enforced is brought into disrepute, and where illegal and bungling
methods endanger the lives and health of growing numbers of women. It provides for the termination of a pregnancy, first, where the continuation of such pregnancy would involve serious risk to the life or grave injury to the physical or mental health of the pregnant woman; second, where there is substantial risk of a defective child being born; and third, where the pregnancy is the result of rape or incest. It provides that such pregnancy shall be terminated only on the advice of two registered medical practitioners.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to address a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Bearing in mind the fact that the security council met yesterday and is to meet again this afternoon to discuss the perilous situation in the Middle East, will the Secretary of State for External Affairs tell the house whether there were any hopeful signs in the discussions which have already taken place?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: MIDDLE EAST-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON SECURITY COUNCIL MEETING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank my hon. friend for indicating that he proposed to ask this question. As my hon. friend knows, the security council met yesterday and will meet again this afternoon at three o'clock to continue its consideration of the situation in the Middle East. It met first on May 24 at the request of Canada and Denmark, and then adjourned until the Secretary General had returned from Cairo and made his report, which was issued on May 27. His report is inscribed on the agenda, as well as an item put on the agenda by the delegate of the United Arab Republic.
Consultations are now taking place with a view to reaching agreement on what action the council might take. Efforts are focusing on the idea of an appeal to the parties to exercise restraint in support of one of the recommendations of the Secretary General based on the following section from his report:
In my view, a peaceful outcome to the present crisis will depend upon a breathing spell which will allow tension to subside from its present explosive level. I therefore urge all parties concerned to exercise special restraint, to forgo belligerence and to avoid all other actions which could increase tension, to allow the council to deal with the underlying causes of the present crisis and to seek solutions.
Yesterday the Canadian ambassador, who intervened in the debate, urged that interim action by the council was desirable along the lines suggested by the Secretary General as a prelude to more specific action by the United Nations later when consultations might, as he said, "allow us to reach a maximum amount of understanding on what the next step should be".
The council will be meeting at three o'clock, and we will have to await the outcome of the meeting this afternoon to see what happens tomorrow or the next day.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Macquarrie) raised a question in regard to an alleged violation of the Canada Elections Act by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation during the week end period prior to yesterday's by-elections.

Another part of the increase is due to the increase in colour programs to the extent permitted by policy, as well as interest on capital loans. These are the chief headings under which the C.B.C. has additional financial requirements, as shown in the blue book.
The office of the Chief Electoral Officer, shown independently from the Department of the Secretary of State, also has an increase in its vote primarily due to a slight increase in staff and to the cyclical salary increases.
On page 328 of the blue book will be found the estimates of the National Film Board. Here again there are increases. I am informed that these increases result from increased salaries including the cyclical pay revisions, the educational film program to meet the growing demand for audio-visual aids in support of better learning and communication methods, more prints for distribution in order to keep pace with the population growth particularly in the 20 largest urban centres in Canada, and also to provide much needed information material for Canadian diplomatic posts abroad, to continue the colour conversion program, and to provide for new distribution offices of the film board in Detroit and Tokyo.
The estimates for the National Gallery of Canada are to be found at page 334 of the blue book. The major reasons for the increase in this vote are more funds for the purchase of works of art for the national collection, the emphasis on major exhibitions and on audiovisual educational materials, salaries for additional positions, cyclical salary review and, for the first time, provision for office furniture and furnishings. During the past year under its new director the gallery undertook a very active program with a view to reaching Canadians everywhere in Canada to encourage them to participate in the cultural life of the nation. This seems to have been very successful, judging by the numbers of people coming to the gallery and the well attended lecture programs. The 1967-68 program reflects the continuation and further development of this role.
The estimates for the public archives and national library are to be found at page 406 of the blue book. The national library and

Supply-Secretary of State archivts building, which was begun recently, has just been completed and we anticipate it will be opened on June 20, so that some of the service requests and reference services which are already being provided will increase at a much greater rate. Some of these are due to Bills C-170, C-180 and C-181, passed during the last session, which resulted in three organizational groups leaving the newly formed Public Service Commission. The bureau of classification revision and the pay and standards branch were transferred to Treasury Board. The pay research bureau became part of the public service staff relations board. The major increases occur in the language bureau and the staffing branch. The language bureau has developed very rapidly and the increase provides for increased classroom facilities, new language teachers, and funds for the purchase of homes and furnishings under the bicultural program in Quebec and Toronto. The rest of the increase is attributable mainly to increased activity in the staffing branch in the areas of travel, advertising and professional services.
This, Mr. Chairman, is a very cursory look at my responsibilities, but I would be very happy to answer any questions. It is hoped that broadcasting will be looked into. It has already been gone into in some depth by the standing committee, which will be meeting on the subject of educational television during the summer. It is hoped that the amendments to the Radio Act will be placed before the house soon, at least for first reading, so the amending bill may be considered during whatever summer recess we are able to have. It can then be discussed by the standing committee in the fall and hopefully the bill, with

any desired amendments, will be passed during this calendar year. As to senior appointments within the C.B.C., it is not now anticipated that they will await new legislation. It is thought the appointments will be made under the old legislation within a relatively short period of time.
The citizenship responsibilities which came under the Department of the Secretary of State on October 1 last have resulted in a bill which I understand will be before the house tomorrow. It was hoped that a new citizenship act could be passed during this centennial year, with all its symbolic significance, but in order to effect some of the really desperately needed changes amendments have been brought forward. It is hoped that whatever minister is responsible will produce a completely new citizenship act in the not too distant future.
During the last year the Department of the Secretary of State has been responsible for some most interesting and relatively unusual preoccupations, one of these being the arrangements for the funeral of the late governor general, and another being the arrangements for the installation of the new Governor General. While they have been the responsibility of the Department of the Secretary of State I should like to say they have been effected mainly by the tremendous efficiency of what is in fact a very small department, and particularly by the under secretary of state. I should like to pay a tribute to him and to his staff for effecting on those two occasions what were really a couple of miracles within a relatively short time.
There will be a number of other protocol occasions which my department will be responsible for when the royal visit takes place in another month. While my department is not responsible for the visit as such, there being a special office set up for it and reporting to the Prime Minister's department, yet we do have certain responsibilities and I understand hon. members will be given some detailed information on this matter within a few days.
If there are questions concerning any part of the department or the agencies for which I am in some measure or other responsible, I should be very happy to answer them.

Mr. Chairman, the severity of my criticism will have nothing to do with the wonderful job the minister has been doing over the last couple of months vis-a-vis the centennial celebrations, but I must say that those of us who are in opposition to the
May 30. 1967

government had expected a rather complete statement on the government's intentions, first about satellite broadcasting and second and more importantly, about educational television.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
The minister rushed in to the house not so many weeks ago with a piece of paper containing the supplementary estimates, and told us if we did not pass them forthwith this would mean the end of educational television for a couple of provinces. As often happens in this parliament, the rush of the moment does not stand the test of closer analysis. I would have thought, however, that whatever was there to support the minister's urgent request of some weeks ago would equally support her statement on her estimates. I will perhaps have more to say about this in a moment, though I should like briefly to examine one or two of the responsibilities of the minister and then, like everybody else in parliament, talk about the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. My comments about the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation will mainly be complimentary.
First I should like to mention the change in the National Film Board and wish the new commissioner, Dr. Hugo MacPherson, well. I think the minister will agree that he is taking over a going concern, and I should like to mention an informal meeting the broadcasting committee held last December at the National Film Board building in Montreal.
The knowledge and concern for the operation of this first rate federal agency of the acting commissioner, Grant McLean, was as obvious to members of the committee as it was remarkable. His knowledge as well as his frankness certainly delighted me, as I am sure it delighted many others who were used to some of the less than frank comments made many times when members of parliament have asked questions. As I say, I wish the new commissioner well, and the fact that he has asked Mr. McLean to carry on and run the board is testimony to the efficiency of that senior official.
This is a good juncture at which to pay special tribute to a senior public servant who has served the agency for so many years, and who for 14 months served the board and Canada in the never easy role of acting commissioner. Our public service and Canada have been fortunate to have had this type of loyalty and dedication.
Supply-Secretary oj State
Let me now break with some members of parliament and talk for a moment about the National Gallery and its acquisitions, and beg my colleagues here to keep their hands off the problems of gallery acquisitions, which should be the responsibility of the director and trustees. When we think of acquisitions we should remember that we are not buying for this year's estimates, for this decade or even for this century. We may be buying, and this is not too extravagant a thing to say, for a millennium. I get very tired of seeing people rushing to the press or other media saying my gracious, we are spending a couple of million dollars on an acquisition; because if this was amortized over the generations it would be an insignificant part of the money spent in this country to acquire priceless things.
We are all jumping up and down about Expo, and rightly so. We do not seem to mind-I certainly do not-that we have been able to find $225 million for that site, and I do not know even whether that figure is correct because it seems to be escalating, to use a new word. If in our joy about Expo we can also think of some permanent acquisitions for the public wealth of this country, then we would not be so quick to criticize when a million or two or even three or four is spent on priceless works of art.
Recently I had the privilege of reading a profile about a rather interesting person, Mr. Thomas Hoving, who did something rather remarkable for the city of New York. He really transformed the parks and other public amenities in that great city. This is the type of support I hope the minister, the gallery people and trustees will have in so far as acquisitions of works of art are concerned. Quality should be the main consideration, coupled with trust in the competency of the officials we put in charge of these public institutions. Whether they spend $1 milion or $2 million matters not over the centuries.
I am glad the minister spoke about the plan for continuing the youth travel program. It is remarkable that 4,800 young people have had the benefit of this program, and many of us applauded the minister when she said the program would be continued. It is my hope that we do not become too self-centred about the program, and I am sure we will not. I am very anxious that our Indian and Eskimo children, for instance, will be given just as many opportunities to visit different places as are those of our youngsters who are, so to speak, in the mainstream of Canadian life.

The minister has made it rather awkward to comment about television because she has just talked about some estimates that have .gone up. Of course they have gone up, and perhaps that should not worry us too much in this expanding field, although I thought for instance that satellites and educational television would be considered. I myself am sort of an old fashioned Bennett Tory when it comes to public broadcasting. Public broadcasting is, among other things, a great monument to R. B. Bennett; and as long as I am representing the constituency of Royal I will do everything possible to continue the primacy of public broadcasting in Canada. Having said that, that primacy must be accompanied by quality and generally speaking I think the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has done a terrific job for this country.
One of the most ironic things about the move to bring French television to Quebec via satellite is that no account has been taken of the very poor quality of French television. French television is subject to almost the severest censorship of any in the world and, if my information is correct, it is boring. If that is what our compatriots want, once the satellite gets into operation they will understand what a really superb job Radio Canada has been doing for Quebec citizens in the field of French programming.
We must not underestimate the wishes and capacities of the people of Canada. When we think of broadcasting I suppose all of us have had examples of criticism about this or that individual program. I cannot help but recall a letter which appeared in one of our local newspapers at home in New Brunswick.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
When the Saturday afternoon or evening, whichever it was, wrestling matches were removed from television some farsighted person wrote and said, "What will the people of Kings county do now that 'rasslin' is off the C.B.C. on Saturday nights?" I think the people of Kings county can find something to do on Saturday nights without watching wrestling matches. This was perhaps five years ago. I do not believe that type of letter would be written now because I think some of the very special work that has been done by the C.B.C. has enriched the tastes of the public. Actually what it is all about here, is it not, is that we as members and the corporation should be challenging the capacity of the public? When we give up the challenge to pap and nonsense we are abdicating this responsibility.

DEBATES	May 30. 1967
Perhaps what I am about to say will be taken as too far reaching but I am going to say it anyway. I remember very clearly, as some hon. members do, the controversy about the so-called "Seven Days" matter. When we had an opportunity in the broadcasting committee to analyse this program we found that of 500 items which had been presented in the life of the program five only were held up to some public citicism. One of them-perhaps this will be the end of my public career but I might as well go with a bang as a whimper -was the matter of the inflating of the breast of the San Francisco go-go dancer. I watched that program and thought it was one of the most poignant and sad events I had seen depicted on television because it was the sale not of any erotic or obscene thing but of a person's dignity. Surely this was the point the program was trying to make. But little people, who have evil in front of their minds, took the wrong context and immediately rushed to the telephone and other communications media and brought the message to their members and to the people who were trying to show what really is obscenity. It was obscene to detract from the dignity of the human individual; that was the message.
I think the corporation should be allowed to continue with this type of challenge. There are many obscenities in life, far more than there are on any newstand down town in any of our cities. There is a very obscene event going on now across the world. There is another one in the Middle East, far more obscene in the true sense of that word than those that we nitpick about in respect of our public broadcasting corporation.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
A person for whom I have a great deal of admiration wrote a letter to the Carnegie commission which has just been investigating public television. In that letter this person said something that I should like to include as part of the comments I make. That delightful essayist, E. B. White, in a letter to the Carnegie commission on public television said:
Non-commercial television should address itself to the ideal of excellence, not the idea of acceptability-which is what keeps commercial television from climbing the staircase. I think television should be the visual counterpart of the literary essay, should arouse our dreams, satisfy our hunger for beauty, take us on journeys, enable us to participate in events, present great drama and music, explore the sea and the sky and the woods and the hills. It should be our Lyceum, our Chautauqua, our Minsky's, and our Camelot. It should
May 30, 1967	COMMONS
restate and clarify the social dilemma and the political pickle. Once in a while it does, and you get a quick glimpse of its potential.
I think the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation does this a good many times, and I believe that rather than denigrate it all the time we would do well to take pride in its achievements. Challenge it, yes, but heaven forbid that I should ever enter the lists in standing in my place in parliament as a critic of quality and content in the narrow sense of programming.
The broadcasting committee has made a recommendation or two which I am sure the minister is considering when preparing legislation. I hope, for instance, that C.B.C. radio will be allowed to get out of commercial activity altogether, with certain exceptions. There are always exceptions that prove rules. We would not, of course, get the opera without the Texaco label, and so on. But I think it is an infinitesimal amount of money that we receive from commercial advertising on radio, and it might provide a good pilot way to get the corporation out of advertising altogether, which perhaps is the ultimate goal of some dangerous people in this parliament, including myself.
In so far as the satellite is concerned, I hope very much that we will follow the Canadian way of doing things and make the agency that controls the satellite a public corporation. I could not imagine the government that sits opposite to me doing anything other than this. This would follow, of course, my Bennettism very well. I suspect that this is what the government has in mind, although we have had very little information about it.
As one who lives on one of the edges of the country, so to speak, I am quick to acknowledge that Canadian broadcasting is unique in the world. I do not make claims that it is the best-it does not really matter what I claim -but I think it can be as good as any if we keep paramount the principles upon which it was founded and nurtured.
One of the things that the corporation does, for instance, for the peripheries of this country is give the public an opportunity to be challenged by criticism and opinion. We have the problem of one-newspaper cities. In some cases the radio and television outlets are run by the same proprietor as is the newspaper. I do not think that inherently there is a danger here, but unfortunately this type of thing prevents a really meaningful challenge to some of the pat ideas of the publisher and the editor, and so on. We in the southern part of
DEBATES	727
Supply-Secretary of State New Brunswick are anxiously awaiting the provision of a new C.B.C. television channel. The private station there is anxious to join the C.T.V. network. I hope that the corporation in its capital budget will soon provide this new facility in southern New Brunswick.
As I said earlier, I believe that the C.B.C. must have a special and primary position within the structure of broadcasting. I want to say what a very great privilege it was to serve on the broadcasting committee. It is an interesting thing to know that on that committee it was not so much the party position that was taken, if there is one

I always feel protected by the heritage I have from R. B. Bennett-but a position on the primacy of public broadcasting. It was not so much the party position as the primary position of public broadcasting. Some day when somebody is doing an analysis of committee reports he may find this an enteresting trend. Perhaps this ground could be explored at some seminar by the C.B.C. itself, on a summer day under a tree somewhere.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
I believe that the profit motive must be subservient to the idea of service in the name of national policy and public interest. Even the president of the C.B.C. himself had to admit before our committee-this was a very crucial admission and, to give him credit, I do not think he liked making it-that there are really very few public affairs programs of national interest broadcast in prime time over the C.B.C. today. This is a serious admission for the corporation to have to make and a serious indictment of our interest in programming itself. The white paper says:
-the determination to develop and maintain a national system of radio and television broadcasting in Canada is an essential part of the continuing resolve for Canadian identity and Canadian unity.
I think that is true, and that is why it is so important to see that a good many programs on public affairs and news, which will serve to strengthen the very purposes for which the corporation is set up, are given prime time. Unless we really mean what we say in the white paper and in the broadcasting report we might as well surrender the whole idea. I do not think the people of this country want that type of surrender, unless I am misinterpreting their views.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
The hon. member for Lotbiniere has asked an interesting question. I think this might be an interim concept leading to the day when we will cease to need relays. I think the minister made a very significant comment in Newfoundland when she said that the French prize-winning play was the first one she had seen since high school. I regret to say that most of us would have to admit the same. I like to look forward to the day when we will not need relays any more, when we will be able to turn on the television and if we come upon a superb French play we will sit back and watch it with understanding, or if it is Monique Leyrac, who is able to do more than any separatist for the advancement of the great French culture, we will be able to enjoy that program also. In the meantime, if relay stations will help to bring about this day, then let us build them.
I did have some important statements underlined but in view of the fact that the minister has not given us her own philosophy on this subject she will have to take the philosophy of the hon. member for Royal. In developing it I should like to quote an article by Eric Goldman called "Can Television Meet The Challenge Of The Future?" The parts I wish to read to the house are very relevant and bolster my argument that many times we underestimate the capacity of the country.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: When was the article written?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
I regret that I will have to supply the reference later. My filing system being as it is, this beautiful Xerox copy is undated. Xerox has not yet achieved a technique for supplying dates on copies of material. Mr. Goldman wrote the following:
-you know perfectly well what commercial t.v. is doing. It is doing what mass culture-whether the dime novels of the 1890's, the movies of the 1920's or today's t.v.-always does: It is catching up certain parts of popular thinking and taste, making them more emphatic and colorful, and handing them back. As such, one can shrug away the effects of t.v. on American civilization. It is, after all, another one of the facts of life.
[Mr. Choquette.J
Mr. Goldman was addressing the United States public. I am far from being a continen-talist but in this instance we have to admit the facts of life in public communication.
He went on to say:
We Americans have our nostalgias, and one of the most persistent is a picture of a premass-communications United States, filled with noble, uncorrupted citizens basing their judgments on an abundant and undefiled spring of facts. Unfortunately the nostalgia is largely nostalgia.
Farther on he wrote:
T.V. has also thrown open windows on the democratic process.
That may seem trite but perhaps in the whole context of my comments its relevancy will be seen. He continued:
-the citizen acquired a far greater sense of the real candidate-
He was speaking of television in elections. I will be coming to the point with which I will end television in the House of Commons.
-the cast of his personality, the temper of his mind, the essential nature of his attitudes.
Of course it was obvious to all of us that it was television which saved the American people once from Richard Nixon.
The author went on to discuss what are the components of the new civilization to which television is speaking. He wrote about the younger generation. Perhaps the emphasis on youth has been done to death. I find it harder to take as the birthdays go by. He wrote about "this youthful, educated, comfortably fixed metropolitan man or woman" in the new America. He called him "the Me-troamerican, with a quite different idea of the kind of life he wants to lead and the kind of country in which he wants to live". I think this is true, and out of it comes a far more compassionate and openminded person. I am not quoting Goldman here; these are my own words. I believe that the young people of today are more compassionate, more open-minded and will not put up with the irrelevant. One of the criticisms I could make of the other generations is that they put up with so much nonsense and irrelevancies. This is why it is going to be so much harder for us as members of parliament in the future. Youth is no longer deceived by all the nonsense, and unless we can show that we too have compassion and an open mind we will, like a good many people yesterday, not do too well in by-elections.
Perhaps the noise over the sound system is a signal for me to stop. Were I to choose a
May 30, 1967	COMMONS
theme it would be that we should stop denigrating the good, that we let the director and the trustees of the corporation buy quality, that we let the programmers in our great national corporation put on programs of good quality in prime time so that they can fulfil their mandate, and that we should not run for cover every time somebody criticizes us. I do not know whether they think members of parliament are producers. Sometimes when I go home and get the full flack from certain programs I wonder whether I should take out a membership in a producers' union or ACTRA. I never hope to stand here and criticize program content because I do not believe that is our job. I do sincerely believe that there is much more good in the public corporation, by overwhelming odds, than there is bad. I think that we-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
The Department of the
Secretary of State must be one of the most all-embracing departments in the government. I notice that the various agencies and branches for which the minister reports are quite numerous. There is the citizenship branch, the Bureau of Translations, the National Museum of Canada, the centennial commission, the office of the representation commissioners, the National Arts Centre, the Canada Council, the C.B.C., the B.B.G., the National Film Board, Public Archives, National Library and National Gallery and the Chief Electoral Officer. I suppose the new Canadian Film Development Corporation should be included. I probably missed a number of the others. I see the Queen's Printer is here, so that is another one. The federal government is unfortunately having very little to do with higher education in the future, and I wish it was more concerned with it. However, with so many agencies and branches one has to make a selection and I will comment on just a few points.
The minister started off by referring to the centennial commission. I think that the centennial commission should receive the congratulations of all members of parliament. It appears to me from what I have seen, read and heard that the commission has done its work very well and that the centennial celebrations are going ahead in a very satisfactory manner.
I think that a special word of commendation should go to the commissioner, Mr. Fisher. I recall hearing Mr. Fisher on the radio a number of years ago, and I must say that it struck me at that time that he was a bit over-enthusiastic in his manner of speaking about Canada. At times I thought it was "a bit thick", but I realized that this man has a genuine enthusiasm and love for the country which he does convey, and I think that a man with those feelings and undoubted ability was necessary to get the centennial celebrations off to a successful start. So he does deserve our congratulations.
The minister referred to the centennial train and centennial caravans. I suppose that every member of the house has received complaints from different parts of the country that the centennial train and caravans did not stop in a particular area for a long time. This is true. I know that there is a schedule to meet for the spring, summer and fall months, but when you consider the number of school children alone in the more populous areas of
May 30, 1967	COMMONS
the country it is just impossible for everybody to see the train or the caravans.
The minister said that the question of their future use is under study. I suggest that at least the caravans should be offered to the provincial museums in each province. A great deal of work has been done to put these caravans together and I think it would be a great pity if they were disbanded following the centennial celebrations. If they were attached to the provincial museum in each province as a permanent historical exhibit they could then be made available by the province on a schedule to travel around to other parts in the years ahead. They could be changed from time to time but, as I say, the basic work has been done and I think they should be preserved.
I was very interested in the remarks made by the hon. member for Royal about the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I do not intend to say very much about broadcasting today. I know that the hon. member for Royal was saying what he believes, but it has always struck me that if you praise some agency, especially the C.B.C, no one in the press gallery pays any attention to you. They much prefer to put in the paper such headlines as "M.P. Criticizes C.B.C." or "M.P. Slashes At The C.B.C.", so that the compliments of the hon. member for Royal will probably not be very widely reported. Nevertheless he spoke as he felt, and I think that this sort of thing should be done from time to time.
The minister said that the appointments to head the corporation will be made shortly. I realize the difficulties because I imagine that the new legislation will provide for different appointments from the kind we have at the present time. The broadcasting committee did make a recommendation that there should be a chairman of the board of governors or board of directors, and then a chief executive officer quite apart from that. I do not know how they are going to handle this problem.
However, Mr. Chairman, it is a good thing that the appointments will be made, because it is probably not a very good situation for the corporation to be surrounded by the air of uncertainty which has prevailed for some time. I believe it is now one and a half years since Mr. Ouimet announced that he would be retiring as president of the corporation.

I think that periodically the head of any public corporation has to say to the legislators that they have their job to do and that he has his and should be left alone to do his job while he is head of the corporation.
The hon. member for Royal mentioned satellites and said that he hoped the minister would make some statement about this subject. I, too, hope that we will have a statement on this subject soon. I would simply underline the remarks he made to the effect that any satellite operation in Canada should be under public control, especially under federal control.
The question of educational television has been mentioned. The broadcasting committee has been expecting to have this subject referred to it for some little time now. It is a very important subject and I hope that the advisers to the minister have not firmed up their ideas too much on this question. The broadcasting committee will be holding public hearings and inviting the representatives of all departments of education in the provinces
May 30, 19S7

Supply-Secretary of State to appear, as well as such other interested bodies as the Canadian Association of Universities and Colleges, the Canadian Association for Adult Education, the C.B.C., the Canadian Association of Broadcasters, and so on. I think it would be very wrong to draft any legislation until these public hearings have been completed and these people who have a very direct interest in educational television have had a chance to be heard.
Apparently these hearings may commence next month and continue in September. The subject is a very important one. However, there has never been any doubt in my mind that the transmission facilities have to be under federal ownership. The question of actual in-school broadcasting can be left to the provincial departments of education. When we get into the area known generally as adult education this is a different matter, and I do not know that this is an aspect which should be left to the provinces.
I hope that before the debate on the estimates of the minister is concluded she will say something about the new Canadian Film Development Corporation. It is some months now since we passed the legislation establishing this new corporation, and perhaps she will give us some report as to the progress which has been made in staffing it. We would also like to know what is happening about setting up a private film industry which it is hoped will be stimulated by this corporation. There is also the very important question of the relationship in the future between the National Film Board and the Canadian Film Development Corporation. I am not going to say anything more about this, but I hope that the minister will say something in this connection later.
At the beginning of my remarks I listed the various agencies for which the minister reports. Some of them perform very different functions so there cannot be any continuity in the remarks I wish to make about them. I want to say something at this point about the citizenship branch, which is one of the minister's responsibilities. A subject which has troubled me and has troubled other members of parliament has to do with the practice in Canada of refusing applications for citizenship and not giving the person who has been refused reasons for that refusal. That might be justified on the first application but it ought not to be permitted to continue forever and ever. Some people seem to be refused forever and ever. Let me cite some examples.

[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
One lady I know of, who is in her sixties and who came from the Ukraine, has lived in Canada for 40 years. She has applied for citizenship three times and each time has been refused. When a person has lived in this country for 40 years, has not left the country and is not likely to leave the country, he or she ought to be granted Canadian citizenship. The logical thing to do with undesirables is to deport them, but surely after 40 years of residence in Canada citizenship ought not to be denied.
Seldom does one know the reasons for the refusal, though sometimes in a confidential way one does learn. We suspect that applications are refused because applicants belong to the wrong Ukrainian organization or they have subscribed to the wrong ethnic newspaper. Often the excuse is as flimsy as that. Or the reason has something to do vaguely with communism. The applicants need not have been communist party members; it is enough if at some time in their lives they belonged to some organization which the authorities believe to be what is commonly called a front organization. This is not just.
I shall go farther. I am not at all sure that membership in the communist party in the past is sufficient reason for refusing citizenship to an applicant. I can think of neighbours and good friends in my constituency who were members of the Hitler youth organization. That was a long time ago. They explained that they belonged to the organization much as one joins the Boy Scouts. Those people fought in the German army. They are good citizens and I am not suggesting they are nazis, but they are Canadian citizens who have been granted Canadian citizenship notwithstanding their membership in the Hitler youth and the German army. I do not think that membership in any communist party in the past should be a reason for denying Canadian citizenship. Besides, the whole question is becoming more complicated every day, there being many different types of communist party. We have the Peking type, the Moscow type and independent parties such as in Yugoslavia. It must be difficult to draw distinctions.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take this opportunity, when the estimates of the Secretary of State are under scrutiny to remind once again the minister of the needs in my riding with regard, first of all, to television.
The Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh) surely remembers that on several occasions in the five years since I have been a member of this house, I have asked the government to take appropriate steps so that the C.B.C. may provide French and English television programs to the various sections of my riding, the most important ones at least, which are still without it.
[Mr. Prittie.l
DEBATES	May 30, 19E7
Mr. Chairman, I am not the only one in this house to face these problems. I know that my colleagues for Saguenay (Mr. Blouin) and for Lac-Saint-Jean (Mr. Simard) have the same problems in their areas. There are also the hon. members for Churchill (Mr. Simpson), for Meadow Lake (Mr. Cadieu) and so many others.
Therefore, this afternoon, I want to renew my request and ask once again the Secretary of State that sufficient funds be made available to the C.B.C. so that its services may be extended to all those areas which surely do not deserve to be penalized by the government because even though if they are remote, they render services to the country by providing it with the raw materials it needs.
Average salaries are high in the Chibouga-mau-Chapais area, a mining district in part, and the people pay a lot of taxes. If they want to take advantage of the services made available to the Canadian people by the C.B.C., such as, for instance, the news and the educational programs, although some of them are not very educational, I must admit, they must pay $200 for a cable which is provided by private enterpise, and $8 a month thereafter, as a subscription, which amounts to $100 per year the provincial tax on communications included. However, I point out to you, Mr. Chairman, that in the Chibougamau-Chapais area, we cannot even get continuous programs because one time we get one channel and another time another, so that it is impossible to follow some serials for instance, which is quite annoying for the people who pay the shot.
In my opinion the government should, as soon as possible, make adequate funds available to C.B.C. so that it may serve those areas. [DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
Indeed, when I happen to discuss the matter with C.B.C. representatives, I am told time and time again that there is no physical problem, but rather a financial one since there is a shortage of money to pay the cost of those services.
Mr. Chairman, there are a few facts I should like to point out to the house, but I see the hon. Secretary of State is absent. Still, as her parliamentary secretary (Mr. Bechard) is with us, I shall acquaint the house with what we have done to urge the C.B.C. or the government to extend those services to our regions.
Back home, there is more than just the Chibougamau-Chapais area; there is also the
May 30, 1967

bush country of Parent-Clova whose people certainly deserve radio and television services as much as other citizens elsewhere in Canada.
Last spring, I had the privilege of heading a delegation from the Parent region which first met the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cadieux) to obtain certain explanations on the ADCOM line, that is the line of national defence, which goes through Parent, and then met the officials of the C.B.C. to find out what could be done with regard to radio and television services in the Parent-Clova area.
Mr. Chairman, during that meeting I learned that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation intended to apply to the B.B.G. for a license to operate a frontier television station at Chapais. That made me happy, because although that was not exactly what the people of Chibougamau-Chapais and Parent-Clova had wanted, nevertheless, it was something better than what they now have, because at least they would have nothing to pay.
It was understood that a frontier station would not be entirely satisfactory, because broadcasts would come late. As far as movies are concerned, it is not terribly important, because generally the films shown on television are of a certain vintage, and whether they are presented a week or two late does not matter much. But the fly in the ointment is the news bulletins and news programs presented on television. Then, it becomes a little embarrassing to hear news bulletins that are late.
Mr. Chairman, the population of Chapais had greeted that news with some joy, but I had other information later on; in fact, right this afternoon, an officer of the corporation said to me that it would be the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation that would make the application and would set up a frontier station at Chapais.
On the other hand, a recent letter from the municipal corporation of the town of Chapais brings to my attention a very different situation and, to let the house know about a point on which there is no agreement in the C.B.C., I shall read that letter into the record, because there is something wrong here and I want this situation brought to light as soon as possible.
So here is the text of this letter dated May 9 and I quote:
Dear Mr. Laprise:
I have yours of April 12 last which was communicated to the members of the town council at the regular meeting of the 6th instant.
Supply-Secretary of State
All have expressed their sincere thanks to you for the great interest you have taken in the problem of television at home.
We would draw to your attention that the license which the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation proposes to request from the Board of Broadcast Governors for the operation of the frontier television station is due to the efforts of the management of Opemiska Copper Mines (Quebec) Limited who are footing the bill so that a local television service may be provided free to the residents of Chapais by means of films and tapes supplied by the C.B.C.
Although this will substantially contribute to the well-being of our community, the programs will not be carried live, but rebroadcast with one or two days delay. The Crown corporation could thus improve the system by giving and paying for live broadcast service to the area so as not to let a private company take over and supply a service which it is not obligated to give and which is not part of its normal operations, although the entire population of Chapais deeply appreciates the efforts of this company, undoubtedly indicative of the highly developed social awareness of the management.
Everyone hopes you will shortly have the pleasure of advising us that the C.B.C. is fulfilling all its obligations to our area by giving a live service and paying for it as it does elsewhere in Canada.
This, Mr. Chairman, reveals a situation quite different from the one that was suggested by the employees of the C.B.C. The latter tell me that the C.B.C. will be establishing a frontier station at Chapais while this letter from the town of Chapais advises me that the management of the Opemiska Copper Mines Quebec Limited will foot the bill instead of the C.B.C. and thus enter into an area which is of no concern whatever to them since they are engaged in a mining operation.
Now, to satisfy its employees, this company is forced to spend money to provide them with a frontier station. Consequently, I should like the Secretary of State to give us some information on this matter, and tell us who is going to provide television services in this municipality.
Mr. Chairman, I would point out to the house that a frontier station at least according to my information, although I am not a technician, cannot serve a region which is more than 10 miles in circumference. Now, since there are about 28 miles between Chapais and Chibougamau, if you set up a frontier station in the city of Chapais, it is obvious that the city of Chibougamau will be out of range.
So, here I am asking for more than a frontier station; I am asking for a direct service supplied by the C.B.C. to the whole population of these two cities, which exceeds 15,000 inhabitants. Those workers and miners

Supply-Secretary of State are entitled to such services as much as any other Canadians.
I am coming now to the Parent-Clova forest region, where the population is entitled to the same services from the C.B.C.
While we propose or try to help the C.B.C. to find a solution to this problem of a signal channel for this region at moderate cost, we are told that to serve isolated regions such as this, the cost would be exorbitant, prohibitive, and we are quoted prices as high as $150,000.
Yet, two weeks ago, in the Parent-Clova area, a contractor from Amos, Mr. Edouard Dufresne, began to set up what is called in technical terms a parabolic system, to pick up the television signals of another station, of another transmitter and to rebroadcast them.
In fact, Mr. Dufresne stated that it would not cost $10,000 to provide the Parent-Clova area with a television station, while the C.B.C. technicians contend that it would cost more than $100,000 for the provision of the same service.
The Corporation's technicians may be contemplating a better service, for whenever they are told about what Mr. Dufresne has done for the cities of Malartic and Matagami and what he intends to do at present for the town of Parent and the area, they say they are not going to waste their time on makeshift installations.
Mr. Chairman, I believe the C.B.C. officials are remiss in their duties. They may have some knowledge, but thes' sit on it and they hinder the development of television in our areas. Therefore, that is what is inadmissible. What private enterprise can do at little cost, the C.B.C. and its officials-here I do not blame only the C.B.C. because it is the same thing with all the crown corporations-need thousands of dollars more to achieve the same result.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
Mr. Chairman, even with a makeshift organization, perhaps, Edouard Dufresne succeeded in giving a perfect picture in Matagami, Malartic and everywhere, even in the city of Alma. Wherever his system has been installed, subscribers get a perfect signal and they are satisfied. I think that the C.B.C. technicians would benefit from visiting Edouard Dufresne's facilities and taking that private business as a model in order to give service at so little cost.
I think that if the C.B.C. wanted to, it could give in the areas I have mentioned here, Parent-Clova or Chibougamau-Chapais, as well as in every area which is still without service in Canada, the services given everywhere else by private or public enterprise.
If private enterprise, such as Radio-Nord for instance, cannot serve Chibougamau-Chapais or the Parent-Clova area, it is simply because it would not be economical to do so. Then, it is up to the government to extend its services to those less populated areas, which comprise communities important enough to justify such expenditures. I would ask the Secretary of State not to make excuses any longer for the officials of the C.B.C., but to provide them with the funds they need to extend their facilities to all those people.
Those are the comments I wanted to make -at least the most important ones-during the discussion of the Secretary of State's estimates.
Before concluding, I should like to make a remark concerning television in the House of Commons. An increasing number of people in our ridings tell us that the debates of the House of Commons should be telecast so that the Canadian people may be really informed of what is happening here.
However-and this is my own personal opinion-if it is decided to telecast the House of Commons debates, all debates would, I think, have to be telecast, and not only the question period. I suppose a channel could be reserved for these broadcasts for those who wish to see what is taking place in the House of Commons at any given time. Those who are not interested could continue to watch other programs.
Of course, that would be very costly and perhaps not very effective. In my opinion, to acquaint the people with what is going on in the house, it would be cheaper to distribute free of charge, on request, a copy of the official report. They would then have a document-and we know that written documents remain. Thus, those who are interested in the nation's business, in the debates, in what his member says or does in the house, would merely have to apply for a copy of the official report of the House of Commons Debates and it would be sent to them free of charge. That would be much cheaper and would give, I think, better results. Televising the debates would interest the people for some time only.

May 30, 1967	COMMONS
To my mind, interest in such broadcasts would soon peter out.
I wanted to state my views on the subject before this idea makes headway, because I realize that across the country, particularly in the province of Quebec, steps are being taken and a publicity campaign being launched to bring the public to demand that the debates of the house be televised.

Mr. Chairman, I also felt that the review of the department we received this afternoon, while covering some most interesting activities of the many that come within the responsibility of this department, omitted any mention of some of those in which we are most interested and which are of great consequence to the development of Canada today. I was particularly pleased to hear the minister mention the dominion drama festival which has, as also have many other causes, been the recipient of centennial grants from the federal government this year.
It gives me a great deal of pleasure to be able to point out to the house that the city of Vernon, which I happen to represent, has through its little theatre, represented western Canada twice in the last three years at the dominion drama festival. It had that honour again this year and the cast and crew were able to make the very extended trip from Vernon to Newfoundland to participate in this year's festival.
Let me suggest that centennial grants should not just be a once in a lifetime occurrence but that the Department of the Secretary of State should consider very carefully the continuing need in this area for future support, mainly in order to overcome the difficulties faced as a result of the geography of this great country of ours. As federal support is forthcoming, and I hope it will be, I hope that the people who set up the regulations for the festival will seriously consider whether the time has not come when the entire part of Canada from Ontario west should be represented by more than one entry. It does not embarrass me at all to say that Vernon's little theatre has been chosen twice in the last three years, as the best entry from all of that territory, but to have but one western entry does seem to be a little out of proportion to the importance of western Canada in the life of this country and to the population that western Canada now boasts. I suggest that a look be taken at the census figures for all of that area, as well as a look
DEBATES	737
Supply-Secretary of State at the encouragement that has been given to drama there, particularly in the province of Alberta with its auditoriums in Calgary and Edmonton, and also in Vancouver with its civic auditorium.
The situation could be changed to broaden the representation from western Canada to at least two plays from that area. At the same time the regulations which are laid down for grants to the dominion drama festival concerning the division between cast and crew should be examined. Anyone who watched the C.B.C.'s telecast, which I think was a rather sad bit of television, would realize the importance of crews, sets and lighting to today's drama. To pretend any longer that five players can travel from one end of the country to the other, accompanied only by a director and an author and somehow present a play that would be considered at all seriously by the adjudicator and audience is a bit of wishful thinking and a relic of the past. I would hope we could have larger federal grants and a somewhat relaxed set of rules for future dominion drama festivals.
Let me join in praise of the centennial commission and the very important work that has been done by that body. We can be genuinely overjoyed at the result of so many of the efforts that have gone into the realization in Canada of this centennial year. I am a bit surprised though about some of the public relations efforts that have reached us by courtesy of the centennial commission.
Let me draw attention to the flip-lidded wastebasket that was provided by the centennial commission community improvement program to at least all members of parliament and I suppose many others in other parts of the country. I am sure that never in the history of publishing has so attractive a container contained so little. Although it may be designed to collect future emissions from this body, if we are to take any warning from what is already inside the prospects for the future are not that much brighter. I know the minister likes to think of herself as being part of the swinging set, but it takes more than the repetition of the word "action" on the outside to convince me that there is much action on the inside.
Let me suggest that in respect of any governmental printing through the Queen's Printer, the archives or any other branch, a serious examination should be made of the policy of dividing pages between the French and English languages. I am all in favour of according equal rights in respect of the
738	COMMONS
Supply-Secretary of State French language in any publication-do not get me wrong in that regard-but I think it is far better practice to design a booklet so that the English is printed separately on one side and the French on the other side. Although it is possible to take both our great national languages and put them together on a page one does not end up with a masterpiece; one ends up with a puzzle.
I am sure most people have not bothered to read "Action" very thoroughly, partly because of the added task of glancing around the page to decide which half is the one you are supposed to read. I thought at one time they might be of some use in schools in French or English language classes, but I am afraid they would not even serve that purpose too well because it is too easy for the student to seek aid from the other half of the column before tackling the problem of translation of the half on which he is working.

I would not have minded so much all this flood of material-this is not the only example of material that seems of precious little use which has come to us from the centennial commission-if I had not had a request from a constituent that I thought was perfectly reasonable. He made it to the British Columbia government on behalf of the Okanagan Historical Society and he says that the result was excellent. We from the west become rather used to British Columbia leading the way, and I would suggest that here is one more area in which that province

Not at all. I am sure the hon. member for Kootenay West knows many areas in which the provincial government has been a leader in Canada. I am sure the coat of arms of Canada is of particular interest to him and that he would be particularly concerned about it. I am sure also that the Leader of the Opposition, who is not in the house this afternoon, would also find this lack in our centennial year a rather amazing one. I hope it is a lack that can be rectified. It is not too late to do so because our centennial year has not yet run its course by any means. I think this is one matter that could be corrected before the year is out.
I know it has been rather out of fashion in late years to include a coat of arms in publications whether they be school textbooks or others. They used to be included in these publications at one time. I can assure hon. members that the coat of arms of Canada, with all its colour, heraldry and intricacy, is a very much "in" thing at the present time and would be studied with considerable interest today, I think, by readers of almost any publication. It is something that should be brought a little closer to the hearts and minds of Canadians.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, perhaps I might tell my hon. friend that while I regret that we do not have copies of the provincial and federal coats of arms to pass out-and I have received a number of requests already this year for them-we now have found a commercial printer who will supply them relatively inexpensively. We are able to give this information to individuals who make requests. Furthermore, the Queen's Printer has had under preparation for the last year a very colourful booklet of the coats of arms and the flowers of the various provinces. It was anticipated that this booklet would be ready by the beginning of this year but publication has been delayed because of the pressures on the Queen's Printer for other centennial publications. However, it should be available fairly shortly. It is in full colour. While it is not loose-leaf in style, I am sure it is a publication that my hon. friend would be happy to send out.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I take some heart from the words of the minister. I find it
May 30, 1967

Supply-Secretary of State picked up in haste because it was about broadcasting in the land south of us. He did find that private broadcasting had not been the disaster that he seemed to think it was a few months ago when we were having discussions in the committee and were drafting the report.
Finally I should like to say a word about a problem I have mentioned before in this session and which was mentioned again this afternoon, namely, the prospects of televising the proceedings in this chamber. It seems somehow that members of this house, members of the press and perhaps some members of the public, certainly the people who work in television, have taken heart from the televised proceedings of the security council meeting the other day when, at a time of great international tension and crisis, we were able to watch that body through television. One hon. member, whom I shall not name, in watching the program said "There is democracy for you". Yet I could not see that it had anything to do with democracy. Certainly very few of the nations represented there know a democracy of the kind with which we are familiar in this country, nor have those representatives been elected to the positions they hold. They were appointed to their tasks.
Neither did we really learn much about the democratic process at the United Nations except how closely that program resembled a sporting event as the television personalities did their best to fill in the dull patches by telling us over and over again that we had come to a singularly dramatic moment in the history of the United Nations and of the world. The camera would then flash back and we would see the same huddle. Certainly no televised football game would ever permit any of its players to huddle so long and to so little effect. I am sure that as the public watched the program they too must have had the impression that this was a game being played and commented upon. This is one of the great dangers of televising something that is like a game but is really a matter of life and death.
Another point which is extremely important and which I think should have been noted by every member of the house, every member of the press gallery, every member of the television crews and of the public who watched the program was how absolutely destructive to the decision-making progress the televising of the security council meeting was. If we had hoped at any time that that group

of men would come to a decision which would further the development of peace in the world, our hopes were frustrated the moment the meeting was televised, because how could any one of them have changed his position with the eyes of a good part of the world watching him and many of those eyes ready to brand him as a traitor to his side the moment he made any change?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question? Could he tell us whether he considers that the presence of the radio and the press at the security council meeting would have been any different from the presence of television cameras? What would have been the difference between the various media of communication?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I am sorry the hon. member is so far behind in his knowledge of the media. I would recommend to him again Canada's prophet, Marshall McLuhan, and his book "Understanding Media" in which the author says over and over again that the media are basically different and that one cannot equate the linear script which we read with what happens through the medium of television, the electronic process. He says that this is an entirely different area and process with an entirely different impact on the viewer. What the press gives us takes at least a day or two to reach us and it takes a certain amount of understanding to follow it. Reading the press is not at all the same thing as watching a group of men, wordless men as they were in this case. I can imagine the overwhelming relief that would have been felt had there appeared a smile of joy on those faces, had they clasped hands and possibly wept and gone back to their places and announced that a peaceful settlement was forthcoming. But what chance was there for this to happen while the meeting was being televised? I would think that the televising of the debates of the United Nations is probably one of the reasons for its relative lack of success and lack of impact and for the fact that the corridors of the UN have become the venues where any sort of agreement that is ever hammered out in that organization is reached.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
May I ask the hon. member another question? What would he say about a radio commentator reporting the proceedings of the United Nations or of parliament? What is the difference between a radio commentator and television?
May 30. 1967

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I do not think radio comment would improve it much either, but I do not think the impact of a radio comment would be as great or as significant or even as damaging to the democratic process as television would be. We have not been sent here to become stars on television. We have been sent here to legislate, and in the case of the UN its members have been sent there to debate. Yet I am afraid the whole business of debating is seriously hampered, and I might even say perverted, when it is televised.

speechtext:
Now, after these few encomiums, the time for criticism is at hand.
Mr. Chairman, the remarks I should like to make to the minister are very mild criticisms -I should say suggestions. First of all, I think that it would be of great interest if the Broadcasting Act, particularly the sections dealing with political programs could be amended in accordance with the views expressed by the Canadian Association of Broadcasters which made very specific recommendations to the committee on broadcasting through its then president, Mr. Jean Pouliot.
May 30, 19fi7

Supply-Secretary of State
Needless to say, Mr. Chairman, that the Broadcasting Act prohibits any dramatization of political programs. But it frequently happens at election time that private stations give to that provision a very restrictive interpretation, which explains why the people, at least in a certain sector, are in the habit of tuning into another station when political speeches are heard on the air, and that precisely because the politicians have their hands tied by the formula set in the act, so much so that political programs generate little interest.
Mr. Chairman, I had the opportunity to call the attention of the house to an incident which took place last year, when the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) known to everyone for his originality, appeared on a television program called "Les Affaires de l'Etat", the French counterpart, I believe, of the program "The Nation's Business". The hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi had then used a very interesting formula which seemed, at first sight, inconsistent with the provisions of the law, because he actually resorted to dramatic effects during that program. In fact, the hon. member was shown in action, driving around in a convertible, coatless and in his shirt-sleeves, greeting his electors, attending a circus, making short speeches, dictating to his secretary. The program was really quite interesting, but if it had been brought before the court, it would have been considered as contrary to the law, because it was clearly a dramatization.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
On the other hand, if the word dramatization must be scrupulously interpreted, then even the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) should be forbidden to appear on television because when he speaks he is quite dramatic. Still, Mr. Chairman, there should be a certain broadmindedness and understanding of the fact that much more latitude should be given politicians when they appear on television. That stipulation on dramatization should perhaps even be deleted and a more dynamic, more interesting formula substituted which speakers might follow during electoral campaigns with a view to reaching the population.
That is the first thing I should like to suggest to the hon. minister.
My second suggestion, Mr. Chairman, which is certainly a moot question and which may raise indeed, strong objections, is that private stations could be assisted-but I wonder to what extent-through grants or
[Mr. Choquette.l

otherwise, and they would be obliged to put broadcasting time at the disposal of the different political parties, when the latter could air their views, not only at election time, but also outside election campaigns.
The problem that arises is that in several parts of the country, let us say in the province of Quebec, there are stations, such as channel 10 in Montreal and channel 4 in Quebec, both private stations, which are precisely television stations with a higher rating than that of the C.B.C., with the result that when the program "Les Affaires de l'Etat" is on the air, the majority of the population is not watching.
Now, I bring this problem to the minister's attention. Are the conditions similar outside Quebec? I do not know, but I am convinced that all the studies conducted so far show beyond any doubt that Channels 10 and 4 have a much larger audience than the C.B.C. and these other stations which, as private stations, do not allow politicians to broadcast their messages or to air their views outside of election campaigns.
There is another item, perhaps a little more controversial, Mr. Speaker. If, as the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Fairweather) mentioned a moment ago, quoting from the Fowler commission report, the C.B.C. is an essential tool for maintaining Canadian unity, I wonder-however controversial this may be -how much longer the minister will allow these conditions to persist within the French C.B.C. network?
All sorts of statements have been made, that information was slanted, that the C.B.C. was infiltrated with extremists-especially in the French network, and more precisely in Montreal. But when those charges are to be substantiated, the matter becomes much more difficult. I remember a very astute answer which the minister gave in the house, saying that people who work for the C.B.C. are entitled to their own political opinions. That was a very sensible answer.
On the other hand, if these political opinions of C.B.C. employees become a source of confusion, then is it not the duty of the government to interfere, or at least to investigate the matter? Because an article was published in Dimanche Matin, a widely circulated paper, saying that all C.B.C. news services, or better, that the information services in the C.B.C. generally, were controlled by separatists.
May 30. 1967

Here, you have a statement of opinion made by one man, which can be expressed. Now, should there be an inquiry?
Should an inquiry be made? The matter could be brushed aside but, only last Friday, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Marchand) himself said that the C.B.C. is full of separatists.
For my part, Mr. Chairman, and this is a personal opinion, I think that if one relates these statements to those of a serious newspaperman and those of a member of the government who observe the situation, then obviously there is no other solution for the government but to undertake a secret or public inquiry in order to ascertain whether the news services of the French speaking C.B.C. network really has an ideological bias. I say this in all sincerity; a public or secret inquiry must be undertaken, because we cannot allow the present situation to continue much longer.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my last remark consists not only what the Fowler commission calls the safeguard of Canadian unity but also a closer relationship between the main cultural groups in the country.
Here is what the Fowler commission says, as can be seen on page 37 of its report; this is a statement of great consequence:
We believe the C.B.C. has failed, and is failing today, to discharge adequately its duties to foster understanding between the two main cultural groups in this country. With rare exceptions, it does not produce programs that would assist English-speaking Canadians to understand the attitudes and aspirations of French Canada. Equally the C.B.C. has failed to convey to French Canadians the doubts, uncertainties, ignorance, and good will of English Canadians concerning the "French Fact".
Mr. Chairman, that was said in 1965 since the report was submitted in that year. That statement deserves a serious and thorough consideration. Is there something more powerful than television? And what is most unfortunate, when the C.B.C. had what is known as a "captive audience", that is an audience that could listen to nothing else than the C.B.C., it did not avail itself of the most wonderful opportunity to get our English-speaking fellow citizens better acquainted with the French culture and avoid, today, all those useless disputes, as well as the appearance of those extremists who frighten us sometimes.
In French Canada, the younger generation may have ideas likely to cause concern. We sometimes wonder who can inspire these ideas 27053-481

Supply-Secretary of State fraught with seeds of revolution? Why has Canada no longer any meaning for them? I am speaking of a certain group, a certain number of the younger generation. Canada is an English-speaking country. That is right. Quebec is a French territory. So, Canada does not exist any longer. It is no longer needed. It is unfortunate that some young people should think along these lines, Mr. Chairman.
It is sufficient to go back to the last election campaign in Quebec to realize that this is true. What were the slogans of the two parties? The Liberal party's slogan was: A Stronger Quebec! L'Union nationale had the slogan: Quebec first! There is no longer any question of a Canadian ideal today, Mr. Chairman, and I say this for the benefit of my Conservative friends. I see that the member for Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard) is here.
Quebec first! Such was the slogan of the present Quebec premier, and when Mr. Johnson was elected, who rejoiced at his election? The member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton). How can he rejoice at the victory of a man whose political philosophy is basically incompatible with the political philosophy of the Conservative party? It is the same Mr. Johnson who said-on this point, I cannot disagree with him because his ideas are somewhat the same as mine-when Mr. Lapointe was appointed lieutenant governor of the province of Quebec, he said: "I hope he will be the last one".
a (5:30 p.m.)
So, he is antimonarchist and the member for Kamloops rejoices at the election of an antimonarchist premier. How can anyone understand that, Mr. Chairman? Such is the series of contradictions to be found among the Conservatives.
On the one hand, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) is against certain bills because, according to him, they are gnawing at the prerogatives of the crown. On the other hand, the member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) introduced a bill which is a visible indication that the man intends to bring down the prerogatives of the crown. There are all sorts of contradictions within the Conservative party.
To get back to my subject, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say that the Liberal party has always promoted Canadian unity, and the best way to bring about Canadian unity is not to thwart anyone or anyone's aspirations.
