Supply-Secretary of State
The only way to give French-speaking Canadians the feeling that Canada belongs to them as much as to other Canadians, and that they are at home in Vancouver is to allow French culture to flourish throughout the country. And what better way is there to bring French culture to all parts of the country than by means of television programs, Mr. Chairman?
And the younger generation is the hope of Canada. The English-speaking young people -I had the opportunity of meeting some of them in Ontario and elsewhere-are interested in the French fact to a really unusual degree. In fact, they show a very keen interest in the French fact. They learn a little French in school, but they do not have the opportunity to chat in this language and to use the knowledge they acquire in school.
They learn French rather as we learn Latin in our colleges, that is to say after five years, we are not even able to ask for a butter scotch sundae in Latin.
The same applies to our English-speaking fellow-countrymen, Mr. Chairman. They learn French, but not in a practical way, because they do not have the opportunity to speak.
Now, if the C.B.C. had some French programs throughout the country, young children coming back from school who have acquired some rudiments of French would hasten to open their television set to try to learn more.
This project would not be costly, Mr. Chairman. It would not be necessary to build a French system throughout the country but only to set up in large English-speaking areas of Canada what is commonly known as repeaters. That would not be costly; as a matter of fact, it would cost less to build some in the large centres across the country in order to bring programs to the vast majority of English-speaking audiences, than what the B & B commission will cost. In addition it would be much more efficient to promote bilingualism in Canada and to enable our English-speaking friends, when they hear French, to consider this language as something else than what we consider Latin.
When we hear priests speak Latin, it is like folklore to us. And yet, we learned Latin four or five years. We have not been taught to use it conversationally. It is the same thing for English-speaking students. They are taught French as a sort of folklore, as a language they do not need +o remember.
[Mr. Choquette.l

However, we still have to know that this exists and it is most unfortunate.
Mr. Chairman, the younger generation is objective and broad-minded and the old fanatisms are about to collapse. When the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Fairweather), who is a true Conservative, spoke earlier, I asked him this: Would you favour the installation of "repeaters" across the country? He replied that he would and I was happy to hear him say so. But had the same question been directed to the Leader of the Opposition, he would have answered in the negative. If the same question were asked to all the front-benchers of the Conservative party, they would answer: "No."
Mr. Chairman, this proves that the younger generation is progressing, that it is the hope of Canada. The best way we can make it possible for that younger generation, which represents more than 50 per cent of the Canadian population, to live better together, is to increase our knowledge of the two great cultures which make Canada a richer country of which we are so proud.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I join with those throwing bouquets at the Secretary of State. I am glad I could throw mine before she left the chamber.
I wish to commend the statements she made about the centennial commissioner. I am proud of what has been and is being done and I second the remarks of the hon. member who referred to the centennial commissioner, Mr. Fisher. I hope the newspaper reports of his being denigrated or of his role being diminished are false. His leadership in the field has been magnificent. He has never been afraid to let his Canadianism show. His verve, vigour and healthy nationalism have inspired the centennial commission and have made its achievements worth while. We are proud that in the commission we have a group of people, headed by Mr. Fisher, who have done so much at a crucial time in our history.
I was delighted to hear the minister say that she will consider what future use is to be made of the centennial train and caravans. After 1967 is over I hope we will still be enthusiastic about them. I hope that in future years we shall continue honouring our past. Most of what has taken place up to now is altogether commendable, though of some developments I am not entirely proud. I was not enthusiastic about the extravaganza, "Sound And Light", and was distressed by
May 30, 1967

increasing difficulty in finding appropriate occasions for the proper and meaningful use of the royal union flag or the Union Jack.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
I am sure many of my learned colleagues on this side of the house and on other sides of the house, if this house has more than two sides, will want to raise many issues with the Secretary of State. I envy her the opportunity she has to give inspiration to Canadians all over the country. I believe that people are right in suggesting that we are going to come out of our centennial year a better country, a wiser country. We are perhaps going to be a little less reluctant to become a bit excited about our own achievements. We have produced in this part of the world a pretty fine political entity. We have men and women in our past of whom we can be proud. We have always pooh-poohed nationalism; we have always been a bit hesitant to get excited about our own accomplishments. I think that the Fishers of this country, and the minister herself when she gets going-she has been showing us lately-will help diminish the self-effacing apologetic attitude which we as Canadians have had for far too long.
I do not think we will react the other way and become so over-confident as to assume our problems have vanished because Expo has been a success and because the centennial caravans and centennial train have been running smoothly. But I believe this is a fine exercise and, generally speaking, I think the minister has done a good job in giving leadership. She has a tremendous department. It is the omnibus department of government. It is a department over which not too much political fire is raised except in connection with the C.B.C. I do not see much pressure exerted to get new books for the library. It is not a gut issue of politics. But if the spirit of the country is all-important it is in this department that the opportunities are greatest.
I end as I began by wishing the minister well in very effort she makes to extend the educational and spiritual life of this country, and I use the word "spiritual" advisedly. She has great opportunities and I will not add to her difficulty by making further remarks at this time.

Inasmuch as citizenship now comes under the jurisdiction of the Secretary of State I wish to remind her that at one time Jack Kent Cooke was associated with Lord Thomson of Fleet in various Canadian enterprises. At that time the two of them were well known together in Canadian business circles. Jack Kent Cooke has now departed Canada voluntarily and has engineered American citizenship for himself almost overnight in the same way that we granted Canadian citizenship to Time and Reader's Digest.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, if I might answer the last question first, I understand Mr. Cooke obtained United States citizenship through a private act of congress, which would be an expensive procedure, I should think, to say the very least, and is a relatively rare one.
May 30. 19G7

Supply-Secretary of State
To my knowledge Canadian citizenship has never been conferred by a private act of the two houses of parliament although the suggestion has been made, particularly by some members of the upper house, that this might happen in what appear to be hard cases where the minister did not have any discretion. I would not wish to encourage this. As hon. members know, I am not in a position to give legal advice to the committee, but as a general principle I think it is pretty well known that a specific act will override a general act, and if that were the will of the two chambers I suppose it could be done. I am not suggesting to my hon. friend that I am encouraging it but I think that as a matter of fact it could be done.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: It would be a long way down the list anyway.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I hardly imagine it could be done by July 1. With regard to the other question concerning the particular item that appears on page 469 of the blue book, "statues and portraits of prime ministers", hon. members will be aware that last year I asked a select committee of knowledgeable people to commission sculptors to begin to fill in the gaps, particularly of the more notable of Canada's prime ministers, and to provide representational statues which might be located on capital hill, in the Ottawa-Hull area, and on these premises.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Parliament hill.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
We hardly wish to have a forest of statues of prime ministers at the end of 200 years, and there being so much beautiful acreage in the public domain in the area it was thought some of these statues might be placed outside the immediate area of parliament.
Recommendations were made and accepted that four prime ministers of this century should be chosen, Meighen, Bennett, King and St. Laurent. The select committee chose four sculptors from various parts of Canada who it was felt would be in sympathy with the individual subjects, and they were asked to present maquettes for consideration. Some months went by and three maquettes were delivered and were approved as to artistic merit by the select committee.
The ministry in general did not view them and to my knowledge has never seen them, but when I viewed them I inquired whether any of the survivors of the three deceased

prime ministers or any members of the families of any of them had viewed them, and I was told that in at least one case friends and relatives had seen it. I want to say nothing about the artistic merit but one of the statues particularly commended itself to me. One of the two others I rejected. The other one I did not like at all personally and it was rejected, but that is neither here nor there.
[DOT] (6:00 p.m.)
The important thing is that if you are going to put up a statue of a statesman it should give succeeding generations an idea of how the statesman looked and how he or she dressed, and the physical attitude should be as recognizable as a photograph. During the centuries there have been many representations of art which have met the test of time and I dare say much of what is produced today, either painting or sculpture, will also meet the test of time. These sculptures are not primarily intended as works of art but as representations to future generations of the statesmen of the past.
Accordingly, and as luck would have it, I rejected the statues of Messrs. Meighen and Bennett. The statues of Mr. King and Mr. St. Laurent may not be everybody's cup of tea but they are instantly recognizable. I am sure all members share my embarrassment in that out of the four the two acceptable on that basis happened to be of members of my own party, particularly since it was my hope that at least these four would be put up this year.
I might add that I was not aware there were any photographs of these maquettes, and I was told they were not easy to move. For that reason they were not even produced for cabinet inspection. I have only seen the photograph of the maquette of the St. Laurent statue. I have not seen the maquette itself.

I do not intend to say anything more but I will listen with interest to any remarks of other hon. members who may wish to exercise their privilege and speak on the motion. At the expiration of this hour I

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say that we agree with the proposal put forward by the sponsor that the Minutes of Proceedings and Evidence of the meeting of the committee last session be made part of the order of reference to the committee, if that is the proper wording, in order that the evidence which was heard will be automatically before that committee. This will obviate the necessity of covering that ground again and having the officials of the company duplicate their activities and efforts. We are the masters of our own rules and procedures, so I am sure we can do this if someone will work out the technique or mechanics of such an order. I am sure no one would object to that procedure.
When this matter was before the house on the last occasion we expressed some concern about the powers sought by the Bell Telephone Company and the necessity of conducting a very thorough examination into the bill and the reason the Bell Telephone Company wants the powers it seeks. If I may be permitted, I should like to say something about the operations of the committee to which this bill will undoubtedly be referred. The nature of the bill is such that we should attach to the committee several individuals who are expert in the field of communications and finance in order that they may advise members of the committee. In this way committee members would be in a better position to understand and fully appreciate the powers which the company seeks.
[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
While this is a private bill and thus, under the rules of the house, relates only to a group of private individuals, I think the operations of the Bell Telephone Company should be considered as a public matter and the law relating to the company should be considered as public law. The Bell Telephone Company is a massive organization. It is seeking to increase its capitalization to $1J billion, which far surpasses the budgetary expenditures of many provinces today. It is involved in the highly developed area of communications and is in the forefront of new developments in telecommunications and electronics. Much of the material and machinery used by Bell Telephone becomes obsolete almost before it is put into use. Virtually every household has a telephone and it is almost a
7S0

May 30, 1967
Private Bills
prime necessity of life for one person to communicate with another. In the whole field of telecommunications, satellites, television and the like there is a state of revolution, and communications have a tremendous impact upon the average citizen.
In view of all these facts it seems to me we would be far better advised to consider enacting legislation relating to Bell Telephone Company as public rather than private law involving only a few individuals as distinct from the general public. The general public is greatly affected by what the Bell Telephone Company does.
Because of the highly technical nature of the company's operations and the extreme complexity of its financial structure, which I do not presume to grasp in even the smallest degree, I also think that the committee which considers this bill should have attached to it a staff of people who are knowledgeable in these fields and can advise its members on just what they should do with this bill. I believe these are prime reasons why the committee should have a knowledgeable staff to advise it. If the government would take cognizance of the desire to make our committees function more effectively than they have in the past, it would take the initiative in giving to the committee the authority to employ staff to undertake the studies necessary in connection with a bill as complex as this one and a company that has such a tremendous influence and effect upon the lives of so many people in this nation. If this is not procedurally possible, or the government does not avail itself of the procedures available at the moment to make these necessary provisions, I hope the members of the committee will recognize the necessity of doing so and will accordingly make the appropriate recommendations or take the appropriate action to enable personnel to give advice to the committee on all the ramifications of Bell Telephone's operations and the bill now before us.
In the last session this bill originated in and proceeded through the Senate. It reached the House of Commons and was given first reading. There was one business meeting of the committee to consider the bill and then the session ended. This time the bill is starting off in the House of Commons. This indicates on the part of Bell Telephone Company-they are very knowledgeable people and pretty smart when it comes to doing things and recognizing authority and power -a recognition that the place to start is the House of Commons because this is where the authority and the power are, and the Senate

comes hindmost in the consideration of this and a number of other private bills that are now before us. I do not know whether this indicates a trend for the future.
As I understand it the fees charged for the introduction of private bills in the Senate are less than those in the House of Commons. I understand that the historical reason for this is that it was thought that the Senate, having relatively little to do and being of relatively little value in the process of enacting law, should be given some sort of function even though a cursory one and accordingly the fees were made less in the Senate than in the House of Commons in the hope of inducing sponsors of private bills to start off in the Senate and let the Senate do the investigative work and study. The House of Commons was ofttimes considered, in respect of private bills, to be a rubberstamp for what took place in the Senate. Perhaps Bell Telephone has recognized that a change is taking place and they should proceed first in the house.
There is another matter I wish to bring to the attention of the house. It relates to the fees paid by Bell Telephone. During the last session they paid a certain amount of money-I do not know how much-as fees to the Senate for the introduction of the bill in that chamber. There was a commitment at the end of last session that in respect of any private bills that were not concluded either by being passed or defeated, those that were merely held up in the works-I refer to any private bills that were still on the order paper -which commitment was arrived at privately by representatives of the parties and indirectly the sponsors of the private bills, the companies petitioning for bills should, if they reintroduced them, not have to pay the fees a second time. I understand that the Bell Telephone Company has paid and perhaps has been required to pay by the rules of the house, which could not be waived until the occasion arose, for the reintroduction of this bill the amount of $150,000 as fees in respect of their private bill. They should not have had to pay this fee.
I hope that one of the first items of business of the committee, after it deals with the matter of staff and personnel attached to it because I think that is of paramount importance, should be to take action in making a recommendation to the house that the fee of $150,000 which Bell Telephone has paid a second time of necessity and through no fault of its own should be returned to the company.

Perhaps the answer I gave to the hon. gentleman who is the sponsor of the bill is worth following up. It underlines the necessity of dealing with bills of this nature, which have such a great bearing and effect upon the general public, as public law because it is only in the House of Commons that we receive a reflection of the public concern about certain matters owing to the fact that we have to go back home occasionally to get acquainted with the feelings of our constituents and at election time to attempt to be re-elected. This, of course, gives hon. members a much better opportunity to express the feelings of the general public because we are, or at least I hope we all are, more closely in touch with the public, its needs and aspirations, than are members of the other place which in many cases is aloof from public opinion and public concern.
So the fact that the Bell Telephone Company has come here, both initially and the second time, underlines the necessity of paying more attention to these matters in the house and, I hope, of taking steps to preserve the public interest rather than to attempt to meet the requests of private citizens in the Bell Telephone Company. In any event I be-

lieve that the $150,000 which I understand the Bell Telephone Company has paid again, should be returned because it was through no fault of theirs that they had to come back here this session.
The powers that Bell Telephone seeks to obtain are extremely broad. It almost wants the right to control the moon and a variety of other planets in outer space. It almost wants the power to print money, distribute credit, and I do not know what else. These powers and authorities which are sought by Bell Telephone are the subject of some concern on our part because in effect when parliament deals with a company as massive as Bell Telephone it gives it the right to promulgate private law by giving it the broad powers which it seeks. This is a matter on which our attention should be centred. Others in our party who have concerned themselves about the structure of the Bell Telephone Company will go into this subject in greater detail.
In closing may I say that I think this bill will be given second reading today. Those of us who are interested in private bills and have expressed concern about the effect which the enactment of such bills will have upon the public have in the past been responsible for delaying the passage of certain private bills. The reason for our concern at times has been the fact that either we suspected or discovered something unwholesome about some private bills. However, as was the case last session, we would like to see the committee given the opportunity to investigate and study this bill with respect to the Bell Telephone Company. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would hope that the sponsor of the bill would give us as careful and assiduous an explanation of the purposes of the bill as he usually does.

maintopic: AETNA CASUALTY COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
I will be very glad to do so, Mr. Speaker. This bill seeks the incorporation of a company under the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act to

May 30, 1967
Private Bills
carry on business in all classes of insurance other than life insurance. A similar bill was first introduced in the last session of the twenty sixth parliament and was passed by the Senate on June 30, 1965, but received only first reading in the House of Commons before that parliament ended. In the first session of the twenty seventh parliament a similar bill was passed by the Senate on February 24, 1966 and had advanced to the committee stage in this house prior to third reading before prorogation.
The proposed company would be a subsidiary of the Aetna Casualty and Surety Company of Hartford, Connecticut. The Aetna Casualty and Surety Company is a corporation carrying on a substantial general insurance business in the United States of America with its head office at Hartford, Connecticut. Aetna Casualty, with its subsidiary, The Standard Fire Insurance Company, writes business in all classes of insurance for which application is being made in the bill to incorporate the Canadian company.
The 1965 premium income of Aetna Casualty, including Standard Fire, increased 17 per cent to $665 million.
The Aetna Casualty and Surety Company was organized in 1907 and operated as a partially owned subsidiary of Aetna Life Insurance Company until late in 1964. At that time a reorganization was effected under which all the shares were transferred to and are now held by a trustee for the shareholders of Aetna Life Insurance Company.
Aetna Life Insurance Company was incorporated and commenced business in 1853. The Aetna Life and Casualty organization now carries on business throughout the United States of America and is one of the largest multiple line insurers in the United States.
Aetna Life Insurance Company commenced doing business in Canada over 100 years ago. In 1960, Aetna Life Insurance Company made an offer to the shareholders of the Excelsior Life Insurance Company of Toronto for the purchase of approximately 70 per cent of the outstanding shares of Excelsior.
Aetna Life Insurance Company presently holds 70.91 per cent of the outstanding shares of the Excelsior Life Insurance Company. Substantially all new business in the life insurance field in Canada is undertaken by the Excelsior Life Insurance Company rather than by Aetna. The Excelsior Life Insurance Company operates with almost complete autonomy, and its operating management is entirely Canadian.

The Aetna Casualty and Surety Company of Hartford has conducted business in Canada for some years and has held a certificate of registry under the Foreign Insurance Companies Act for the past 48 years. A substantial part of the business conducted by the Aetna Casualty and Surety Company has been related to business conducted by the company with United States corporations having subsidiaries operating in Canada. A certain amount of direct business has also been carried out, especially in connection with major risks, an example of which is the liability insurance for Expo 1967. The company has not maintained any offices, other than for the servicing of claims, in Canada but has carried on its Canadian business through its chief agent, Dale and Company of Montreal.
The Aetna Casualty and Surety Company has reviewed its operations in Canada and has concluded that it would now be desirable that its direct Canadian business should be carried on by a company incorporated in Canada. It is believed that this step would enable the Canadian operations of the company to be developed more effectively and with greater Canadian participation in the conduct of the business.
In anticipation of expanding its operations in Canada, either through a Canadian company or through the United States company, Aetna Casualty and Surety will establish an office in Toronto. It has already selected a Canadian to be general manager of its operations in this office. Another Canadian has been selected to be in charge of the fidelity and surety operations.
[DOT] (6:30 p.m.)
The establishment of a Canadian company would provide additional insurance capacity for the Canadian market. This would be true with respect to all classes of business which the company plans to write, but is particularly important in the surety bond field because of the vast construction projects which are planned for Canada in the future.
The Aetna Casualty and Surety' Company of Hartford now has claim offices located in Toronto, Montreal, Quebec city, Hamilton, Winnipeg, Calgary and Vancouver with approximately 40 employees located in Toronto and another 50 spread throughout its other claim offices in Canada. All but four of the present employees are Canadians, and all present employees would become employees of the Canadian company. Normal growth would indicate that by the end of five years employees would number 300, of which at
May 30, 1967

least 95 per cent would be Canadians. The Canadian company would be under the direction of the before mentioned Canadian general manager, who would have charge of the company's operations throughout Canada. Initially, underwriting, sales, engineering and accounting would be centralized in the head office in Toronto, but as need becomes evident these facilities would be placed in other important cities in Canada. Of course the experience and services of the Hartford company will be available for the assistance of the Canadian company.
As is customary for any prudent insurance company, it will adopt a re-insurance program designed to protect its surplus from catastrophic loss.
A financing plan has been developed to provide the capital and surplus necessary without impairing the balance of trade position of either Canada or the United States.
It is the intention of the Aetna Casualty and Surety Company, as the parent company, to leave any underwriting profits in the Canadian company to strengthen its financial structure.
A primary objective for the company, already demonstrated in the selection of the general manager and the manager of the bond department, will be to employ Canadians in the management of the operation to the extent that they are available. Of course all of the clerical personnel will be Canadians.
The establishment of this Canadian company will create for Canada additional employment, additional capital funds and, as previously mentioned, additional capacity for the insurance market. The Aetna Casualty and Surety Company has stated that it looks upon the establishment of the company as an additional thrust for the already demonstrated expanding Canadian economy, and as a permanent and growing part of this economy.

maintopic: AETNA CASUALTY COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
As the
sponsor of the bill has already stated, this bill does have a rather familiar flavour because we had a look at one which was essentially the same during the previous session. It immediately comes to my mind that one could, in effect, label this as the A to Z bill, but since the sponsor is a firm from the United States perhaps one should say the A to Zee bill. In the clause which sets out the classes of insurance which it is proposed this company will handle, it so happens that every letter of the alphabet is covered. As the sponsor says, apparently everything is in here that one
Private Bills
could imagine except the carrying of life insurance.
I should say at once, Mr. Speaker, that I listened carefully to the very straightforward outline of the purposes of the bill given by the hon. member for High Park (Mr. Cameron). In my opinion the speech he has just delivered constitutes a convincing argument as to why this bill should not receive passage in the house. He has been quite straightforward in stating the company will be a subsidiary of the United States company, and that while they have been operating in Canada in the past directly, the passage of this bill would enable the company to expand their operations in this country.
I believe this statement raises at once a rather fundamental matter of economic policy so far as the country is concerned. I must say that in the insurance business, and in the financial field generally, it is my view this parliament should accept the view that foreign enterprise in this field should not be encouraged to expand at this juncture in our history. The hon. member for High Park, who is sponsoring the bill, obviously holds a somewhat different point of view on this question. In my view the presentation of the bill does open up, some very broad considerations concerning the economic future of this country.
I think it would have been quite appropriate if the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Gordon) had been in the chamber during this hour to give us the benefit of his views on the proposals in the bill. I am sure that with his background and experience as a former minister of finance in this country, and with the knowledge we have of some of the views he has expressed in this chamber and in other places in Canada, he would be much more competent to go into the ramifications of this particular bill than I feel I am.
Nevertheless, while I certainly do not agree with all the proposals that have been made by the President of the Privy Council with respect to controlling the increasing subservience of our economy to that of another country, I do agree with what I feel should be his basic objective, and that is to adopt measures to guarantee the economic independence of our country. The proposal contained in this bill moves in exactly the opposite direction, and it does so in a field which has been recognized in our banking legislation as being one about which not only the President of the Privy Council and members of the New Democratic party are concerned, but even the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) has

May 30, 1967
Private Bills
indicated increasing encroachment and control in the financial field as something which should be of concern to us all.
I suggested in previous discussions on insurance bills that in my view insurance companies are not wealth-producing institutions. When we discuss the principles involved, allowing foreign financial institutions such as insurance companies to extend their operations in Canada, what we are in fact doing is enabling an institution to draw out from Canada wealth which is being created by all of us.
I think there is a valid distinction between the extension of an operation of this kind in our economy, and an investment which may be made in the resource extraction industry. I think it should be clear that in expressing this point of view I am not in any way casting reflections upon the particular company which, as the sponsor says, is an old established firm in the United States. I am not casting any reflections, either upon the way they have operated their business, or upon their financial soundness. Nevertheless this measure does involve a real question of policy that I feel puts us in the position of having to discuss the question from the broader point of view than the incorporation of this particular company.
[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker-and statistics bear this out-that there has recently been a very deliberate attempt over a period of years on the part of United States firms to move into and gain increasing control of the insurance business in Canada. The sponsor of the bill mentioned that there had been a purchase of a former Canadian company, and this is just one example that has been repeated many times in recent years of a process that has been going on, to the point where, in this field as in so many others, we as Canadians, either in this parliament or outside of it, are not going to have any real say in the conduct of the affairs and economic life of Canada.
I am not at all certain that one should be concerned whether a company of this nature is going to undertake a single class of insurance business, or multiple classes of insurance business as proposed in the bill. I suppose that if this company is going to operate in that field, it should be able to write insurance covering all kinds of possible damage or hazards to property. Nevertheless the fact remains that there are now in operation many businesses which provide Canadians with the opportunity of acquiring the insurance that they may desire to place upon their property

in order to protect themselves against the financial loss that may occur as a result of fire, accident, falling aircraft,, earthquakes, explosions, or any one of the other classes mentioned in the bill.
One of the classes that is not mentioned in the bill, one which does cover damage from earthquakes, and a class which, if it had been included and the company were prepared to confine its operations to this field, might have led me to support it, is tidal wave insurance. I mention it because part of my constituency was damaged a few years ago by a tidal wave which had been caused by an earthquake in Alaska. Quite considerable damage was done at that time to property.
As a result of this occurrence I discovered that apparently tidal wave insurance is not available to the ordinary property owner. If the sponsor of the bill could persuade this company to withdraw these other classes of insurance and to confine itself to providing tidal wave insurance, perhaps I might be convinced to take a different position on the bill. Because this is an example of the kind of protection which apparently is not available, and there might be some virtue in a company entering this particular field of insurance. Although these other hazards are covered, apparently this particular one is not.

My colleague suggests that there are perhaps not enough letters in the alphabet. Those of us who have been here for some time know that you cannot go from (aa) and (bb) down to (xx) when enumerating paragraphs in the interpretation clause of a particular bill, though I do not suggest seriously that this is a reason for this or any other company not offering this particular class of insurance.
At times, Mr. Speaker, I am amazed by the willingness with which Canadians enter arrangements to become directors and operators of wholly owned subsidiaries of firms outside Canada. I think that the particular elements in our society that move into and operate in the field of business management and the framing of business policies should, by right, be among those who are most concerned about preserving the economic viability of the Canadian economy as something which belongs to Canadians. I suppose it is part of the philosophy that is all too prevalent, that we are too willing to make a fast buck at any price.
May 30, 1967

I think this attitude and outlook enters into the approach that people in the business community are inclined to take, sometimes subconsciously, without really realizing the implications. I suppose one could argue that we are moving into the field of a type of international corporate structure; but in our particular situation this is a pretty one-sided operation because we lie next to a nation as large and wealthy as the United States. In the process is seems to me we are likely to be so completely submerged that any meaning in reality to Canadian life will go down the drain. This is what will happen if we in this parliament do not show our concern about the trends which are becoming increasingly evident all the time.
I do not know, Mr. Speaker, that there is much more I can add to my argument. I am not too hopeful that I can convince the sponsor of this bill of the error of his ways. I know he has put forward his proposal in good faith, and I presume with an honest conviction that it would be in the interest of Canada and would be expedient to adopt this bill. I simply say to him in closing that he and I apparently have a very honest difference of opinion as to what in this sort of situation is in the real interest of the economy and the citizens of this country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have always had a great appreciation of the abilities of my colleague the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett), but after listening to him I think the word appreciation is rather pale and insipid. He has just given me cause to admire his perceptiveness and his ability to follow the highly detailed, technical and complex remarks made by the bill's sponsor. My colleague grasped the significance of the document introduced in the introductory remarks by the sponsor of the bill. When my colleague referred to that document and said that he appreciated the straightforward manner in which the bill's sponsor had outlined its purposes, I was amazed. I had not thought it possible to follow the labyrinthian course that the bill's sponsor outlined when he explained the intricacies, complexities and involvements of this company with other companies.
* (6:50 p.m.)
As the bill's sponsor spoke I was reminded of the mazes we tried to solve in the Saturday newspapers of long ago, when we were children. One had either to find the starting point to solve the maze, or begin again. The ability of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni to
Private Bills
find a solution to the maze presented by the sponsor of the bill surprised me. As for myself, I must read Hansard and study it in detail to appreciate the full implications of this bill, the corporate structure of the company, and to try to assess its affect on the public of this country.
It is clear that the company spoken of in the bill is not Canadian owned but is a subsidiary of a United States company, as are many insurance companies and the like in Canada. Some years ago when Mr. Barrette was premier of Quebec and Mr. Jean Lesage was running the campaign of the Liberal party, which was then in opposition, the Liberal party's clarion call was the slogan "maitre chez nous"-master in our own house. This was more than a declaration; it was a symbol of the feeling of the Liberal party in Quebec, that the people of Quebec ought to be masters in their own house. That slogan is one which the national Liberal party could also use. Canada ought to be master of its economic house. If we are not our own master, if we are not vitally concerned in owning our own house in the economic sense and stopping the drift to a greater foreign control of our industry and commerce, we shall not long be our own political masters. He who controls his purse controls his destiny.
No other nation in the world has such a high proportion of its industries and commercial establishments controlled and owned by foreigners as has this nation. I have heard varying figures mentioned but I believe that somewhere around two thirds to three quarters of our total economy is under foreign control, under the dictation of people who are not Canadians and do not live in the country. The Aetna Casualty Company, or whatever the name of the parent company at Hartford, Connecticut, is another example of a foreign company owning part of Canadian commerce.
My colleague for Comox-Alberni spoke of the philosophy of the President of the Privy Council when he was a private member, a candidate, chairman of a royal commission, a budding author, minister of finance, again a private member, minister without portfolio and now as President of the Privy Council. I shall not repeat what was said. The views of the President of the Privy Council are well known. Unfortunately the Liberal party does not espouse the slogan "maitre chez nous" -except for the Prime Minister.
Some time ago on a nation-wide television broadcast the Prime Minister enunciated his

Supply-Secretary of State philosophy and the philosophy of his government. He said Canada ought to regain and own an increasing proportion of its industry. We thought he meant what he said. Considering the new legislation which demands that new life insurance companies be Canadian owned in majority, and the statement of the Prime Minister, we took his forthright statement to mean that the principle enunciated in the life insurance legislation would apply to other insurance companies.

item in my departmental estimates concerning the expenditure for prime ministers statues. I hope I shall be able to pick up in a coherent way the thread of what I was saying.

In fact, since the photographs were published I have received nothing but commendation on my decision, not, I hasten to say, because there was anything lacking in the aesthetic merit of the works, or the quality of the artistry, but only on account of the manner of representation.
Some notable modern sculptors, of whom I suppose Mr. Gerald Gladstone is the greatest example in Canada, indicated that in their view a feeling for the character and personality of the individual represented might be more appropriate. I have asked that the expert committee be reconstituted and be requested to select two more artists who will be expected to produce more representational figures. This time, so that there may be no

controversy about their artistic merit, I have suggested I will see the maquettes when they are ready, and myself decide in the first instance whether or not they appear to be sufficiently representational. Only if they pass that test would they then be considered on their artistic merits. As far as I am concerned this is acceptable to the expert committee, which is at least in the process of selecting two more sculptors. The latest information I can obtain is that at least a sculpture of Mackenzie King may be ready during 1967. Sites were selected on the grounds of the parliament buildings, on the grounds of the Supreme Court building, and I believe one was to go on Nepean Point. However, I cannot tell the committee which ones were to go where, but subsequently I will be able to give a better report.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
For the reasons I have explained, I do not know what the individual statues were to cost.
The portraits referred to are those of two leading personages, one the Prime Minister and the other the former prime minister, the right hon. Leader of the Opposition, who have not heretofore been painted. It will be noted that outside this chamber a painting of Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent appears. Some months ago I wrote to the right hon. Leader of the Opposition, and to the Prime Minister, suggesting a number of artists' names, who are well known, and who had within the last two months painted prime ministers, speakers and other notables, and suggested that from this short list, or from any other source, these individuals might arrange to have their portraits painted now, while they are in blooming health. Of course, neither of these portraits would hang in the parliament buildings while the subjects are still members of parliament, or members of the other chamber. Only upon their leaving parliament would their portraits join those of other prime ministers.
It seemed to me it was an appropriate time to obtain these two paintings, and for once to give the objects of the paintings the opportunity to select their painters. 1 ascertained over the dinner hour that the portrait of the Leader of the Opposition is in process but, though the Prime Minister had a picture painted by a volunteer artist, it was not considered suitable for the specific purpose of hanging in the halls of parliament. Accordingly, the Prime Minister has been urged to make himself available to a portrait artist with all reasonable dispatch, bearing in mind
Supply-Secretary of State his other responsibilities, in order that his portrait might be painted.
That is the saga of the statues. I am not sure whether in the future it is likely that all prime ministers will be sculped after a decent interval, by virtue of the fact that nowadays it is not thought to be a good idea to have a forest of stone rising around parliament buildings.
A number of suggestions have been put forward, including the dedicating of fountains, something which hardly seems to be appropriate to the name of a former prime minister. There have been suggestions that a sculpture garden with at least busts, for instance in the sense that one sees in Rome, might be considered for the capital area, with prime ministers and perhaps other leading Canadians to be sculped from time to time. These are rather expensive. I think the last one done was by a Toronto sculptor. It was donated, but the pedestal alone cost something like $60,000. It seemed to me that the centennial year was a particularly auspicious one in which to begin filling in the sculping of some of the men who have caused the modern state of Canada to develop as it has. Accordingly it was thought parliament would be prepared to honour these gentlemen in this way by having them sculped. That is why the Department of the Secretary of State undertook to do the work.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to thank the Secretary of State for the full replies she gave to what I thought were two short questions just before the six o'clock adjournment. I do not intend to speak on the C.B.C. on this vote. I am going to speak at some length when the C.B.C. vote itself comes forward, which may be in a few days; but I do want to comment on some remarks made in this chamber this afternoon in the course of the discussion on the estimates of the Department of the Secretary of State.
This afternoon the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke was passing some remarks about televising the proceedings of the security council and intimating how this would give the entire world the impression they were taking part in running world affairs. The comments he was making with regard to the printed word were not entirely commendatory and they did not rest easily with me, who has been associated with the printed word for the past 40 years, and my father before that.
How in the name of heaven does the hon. member expect the world to see the televised
758	COMMONS
Supply-Secretary of State proceedings of the security council or of any other legislative body that he thinks should be televised? Are we all to stop work to watch the television screen? People still have to earn a living, and according to the time zones in this world people have to sleep at certain hours, people have to work at certain hours, and people have to eat at certain hours. Yet we are told the impact of televising legislative proceedings would be terrific, that the world should be able to participate in the deliberations of legislative bodies, and that the only way it can feel it is taking part is through television. I tell you, Mr. Chairman, the world still has to earn a living, it still has to rest, and people like recreation of various kinds at certain hours of the day or night. The fact is that television binds us to the time the television proceedings are on.
I cannot for one moment visualize the world stopping breathing just to watch the televised proceedings of any legislative body; and I thank God for the printed word, which makes it possible for us to get accurate, and fully detailed reports of proceedings throughout the world. Those reports can be read at the convenience of the reader, not at some time specified in advance by some deliberative body meeting in Geneva, New York, London, or Paris, France, at the convenience of that body, no matter what the time zones elsewhere in the world may have the residents of those zones doing.
I cannot subscribe to the opinion that television is so far superior to other means of communication that the world should stop whatever it is doing just to watch it; and I thank heaven for the printed word which gives us an accurate report, one to which we can refer days, months, or years later if we wish. In television you have it for one instant, and then it is gone.
The hon. member for Chapleau this afternoon was standing up in his place and asking that the Canadian Broadcasting government-and "government" is not a bad slip of the tongue, because they do what they very well please-that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation should be given all the money necessary to provide radio and television services in what he calls the frontiers of the nation. The estimates this year for the C.B.C. are up $29,476,000, to a record $143,960,000. Yet the hon. member for Chapleau says that the C.B.C. should have all the money it needs to take television and radio to the far, outlying parts of this great country of ours.

DEBATES	May 30, 1967
In the name of heaven, does nobody pioneer in this nation any more? This nation was built up by people going out to the frontiers, developing mines and farms. They did not have television and radio paid for at other people's expense. They had fiddles and pump organs. They had musical instruments. They read books, magazines, and newspapers, weekly or daily as the case might be, and they opened up this country in the way it has been opened up. It is a credit to them, and I only hope we can measure up to the fine people who made this country what it is today.
e (8:20 p.m.)
The hon. member says television and radio entertainment should be provided. I point out that Marcel Ouimet says 62 per cent of the C.B.C. programming is entertainment. In other words, entertainment takes 62 per cent of this $143,960,000 which we are going to be asked to vote for the C.B.C. But more of that later.
Right beside the hon. member for Chapleau is his seatmate, the hon. member for Rober-val. I sat in this house that morning until three o'clock or 3.20 when adjournment was being held up because of a desire to have a milk subsidy of $5 or $5.10. I have never been certain whether it is $5 or $5.10, because the farmers carried signs asking for $5, yet all the discussions I have heard have made reference to $5.10. How in heaven's name can we expect the Liberal government to provide a milk subsidy of $5.10 and also provide radio and television facilities to all the frontier areas of this nation, no matter where one goes in this country to make a living according to his own whim-I am thankful it is a free nation, but the Creditiste members will not find it possible for us to pay $5.10 in milk subsidies and in addition increase grants to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation as outlined by the hon. member for Chapleau.
I find it passing strange that two hon. members in this house who are seatmates should ask the government to pour out the money in two such divergent ways. I think we must think occasionally about the taxpayers, and I admit there are not many in this house who do. We must consider the person who is carrying the load both for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and the federal milk subsidy.
Where is this French culture everyone is talking about? We hear a great deal about two cultures in this nation: There is only one culture, the world over. Civilization is the sum total of cultures in all parts of the world.
May 30, 1967	COMMONS
There is no such thing as biculturalism. I am wondering what culture these Creditistes are talking about. Are they talking about the culture of the past which built up this nation when the people had fiddles, hand instruments, organs and the like, or are they talking about the culture associated with television and radio, through which we are now going to open up the country? It will be interesting to know which culture they hold in the highest regard, the old culture of the past or the new culture of radio and television.

Mr. Chairman, while it would be tempting to comment on some of the remarks just made by the hon. member for York-Humber, I think I will deprive myself of that luxury this evening and confine my comments to matters relating directly to the estimates before us.
At the outset may I raise a question, and I suppose this is the only time one can ask questions which are borne out of the innocence of naivety or the early stages of one's involvement in enterprise. One of the incongruities which has disturbed me since becoming a member of this house is that, while we are ostensibly discussing the estimates contained in this blue book, they are the last things in the world that get discussed either in the house or in the committees.
I shall do no less in this regard than any other member in this house, because I think part of the difficulty in dealing responsibly with the massive spending that is carried on year by year by this government results from a lack of information on which to assess in any kind of rational manner whether the spending we are being asked to approve is necessary.
I am glad to say that I have learned recently from one or two departments that the officials themselves in various departments have become quite concerned about this lack of information and intend to put in some detail about the spending that takes place. This is something which will not cost the departments a great deal of time, energy or money. At this time I believe that every Crown corporation presents an annual report. These reports are quite costly, at least by Prince Edward Island standards. They are not run off on a mimeograph machine over a week end. Very often pictures are used for emphasis, and many other means are used to make this a presentable document, although often they are void of any hard and useful
DEBATES	759
Supply-Secretary of State information. More often than not these annual reports appear to be public relations documents. I suppose this is necessary on occasion to sell the services and wares of these various departments. It is my feeling however, that when we are called upon to act responsibly in deciding the value of the expenditures of various departments we should be given more information.
Frankly, I find it quite shocking that in certain cases we are called upon to vote large sums of money without having been given adequate information. Having regard specifically to the estimates of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, we are given very little information. This year we are being called upon to agree to the expenditure of some $140 million and are told in three succinct lines that this is simply a grant in respect of the net amount required to discharge the responsibilities of the national broadcasting service. I suppose that explanation is given year after year without being changed by one jot or tittle. We are not even told the number of employees required, as we are in relation to some other departments. These employee positions are now euphemistically termed "Positions (man-years)". I hope somebody will give us some explanation as to that particular designation.
It is my belief that if we are going to treat these estimates sensibly and rationally year after year, both in the house and in the committees, these large amounts of money should be broken down with specific detail. It may not be necessary to print those details in a fancy book or in a book at all, but surely the department should be able to give members of parliament this detail in order that we can relate our discussion to the specific items and perform the job we are here to perform, namely consider the finances of government.
Let me now mention some of the various areas of responsibility encompassed by the Department of the Secretary of State. I suppose I should take the time to commend the minister for the capable way in which she seems to have handled a great many of her responsibilities. Certainly she has one of the most interesting portfolios of government, although not an easy one. Indeed I wonder whether it would be possibly for her to remember in an instant all the various programs, corporations and plans for which she is responsible.
In reviewing her remarks of earlier today, I am disturbed to note that she did omit, as has been pointed out, three or four subjects which I think are of importance to us. The first of
COMMONS DEBATES	May 30, 1967
Supply-Secretary of State
these, which has been of interest to me for some time, is the Canadian Film Development Corporation. When we were asked to approve of the establishment of this corporation as quickly as possible there seemed to be great urgency to put the legislation on the books. The legislation has now been on the books for some time, yet this whole activity both publicly and privately has been almost as dead as a nit.
I am inclined to speculate that one of the reasons for this inactivity is that during the early stages the government was anxious to have this legislation become operative in order to produce a round of centennial films. That is a commendable enterprise, but as I have mentioned privately to the minister and others, I hope we have not established a corporation on the basis of a one shot affair, and that in fact we have established an agency to encourage a vital cultural development, which could be tremendously meaningful to this nation.
While many of us may think of a feature film as being purely entertaining, there is something about the nature of a feature film which reveals to members of that country and to others a great deal of the personality of that country. The feature films can at the same time be a valuable source of entertainment. I hope we will not have to wait too much longer before positions are filled on this important corporation, or for the necessary regulations to be laid down so that this corporation can come into effect. We have waited for a long time now, and I speak in terms of years, for something to happen in this important sector. Having passed this legislation, I do not think it is necessary for us to wait much longer.
I should like to refer briefly to another matter of great interest, and I refer to the subject of satellites. It is perhaps putting the cart before the horse to spend a great deal of time, as we have done and will do, discussing the C.B.C. and the proposed amendments to the act, when in fact the development of satellites may spell out the death knell to the C.B.C., as we have known it. If by the development of satellite communication in this decade we open up the opportunity for people to tune in any time anywhere to a variety of programs from various sources, our control of broadcasting through the C.B.C. will be greatly reduced.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
I think it is folly for the government to delay, or at least seemingly delay, referring 
this important matter to the appropriate committee. It should begin in every way, shape and form possible to accelerate our involvement in this program. There are countries with a great deal of vested interest in controlling our communications sector, and if they steal the march on us in this regard it will not be to the credit of this government in the years to come.
Then there is the matter of educational television. This is a complex field, and' I do not pose as an expert in it or even as one who has strong opinions. However, I believe, as was echoed earlier by the hon. member for Royal, that since this question was of vital significance to the minister earlier this year, it is high time it was given serious study by the house and its committees.
Then of course there is the National Centre for the Performing Arts. I really did not expect the minister to refer to this matter in her estimates. There has been a joke going around here for some time, that we could not tell the National Centre for the Performing Arts from a hole in the ground; but we cannot say that any longer because it is above ground and we know that activity is taking place there. I am a little disturbed, however, by comments made recently in the city of Ottawa, that this particular centre may not be as available for the encouragement and development of local culture in Ottawa as I would like to see it. I realize that we are constructing a centre that will serve all of Canada, but I think we are realistic enough to believe that it will provide some special service and will have some special significance to Ottawa, Hull and environs. Therefore before too long I hope a public discussion will take place as to the actual progress being made with this tremendous cultural complex, that will be fully operational in our midst before too long, we trust.
Then there is the matter of the centennial youth travel program. I, like other hon. members, feel this has been a tremendous program and I am glad to hear it is not going to be dropped. I have been somewhat disturbed at aspects of the administration of this program and to learn that they have got out of hand. Through personal contact with and involvement in one specific request of a youth group I have noted that there seems to be either too much bureaucratic jungle, or perhaps the staffing requirements are not adequate to meet the kind of request that is being made.
I trust that as the program continues to develop the situation will improve. Perhaps
May 30, 13S7	COMMONS
there is not as much reason for a poor show in this regard, administratively, as in others, since it has been in operation three years. If expertise is not available or adequate, I hope that interested parties are being communicated with so that this matter may be attended to at an early date. Generally, Mr. Chairman,
I want to commend the minister and the centennial commission for a program that has done a great deal to foster a real understanding by young Canadians of what their country is really like.
There has been reference here today- though I had not originally intended to speak on the matter-to the possibility of televising and broadcasting the proceedings of this place and its committees. I have found some of the discussion today rather confusing. I find it a little disturbing that a person in this place, who by his very appearance here or position here is involved in the democratic process, would be afraid of allowing people to see what is going on in this important deliberative chamber. I for one believe that the more communication with and the more opportunity we can give people to understand what happens in this place, the better we will perform our jobs and the more participatory will be the democratic system that we hope to see foster and grow in this country.
It disturbs me that in this connection we have been so neglectful of two media as to discriminate against them. I think without question we have allowed for years those who work for the newspapers to have ready access to this house and our committees; but for reasons which are mostly myths, I think, we have deprived the media of radio and television from having the same equality of access to this chamber and our committees. While I am on this point-

You may ask it in a few minutes. While I am on this point, Mr. Chairman, I would like also to mention something with regard to technical innovation, which I believe will be exceedingly important. A few years ago, if I recall correctly, the then prime minister had made available in his office a rebroadcast, or a speaker system so he could hear what was happening in the House of Commons. As I understand it, there was a great disturbance about this and eventually that system was removed. I thought that was a great mistake. I think if wiser counsel had prevailed those who had been
DEBATES	761
Supply-Secretary of State alerted to this possibility would not have argued for the removal of one speaker but for the installation of one in every member's office in this place. Indeed, I would pursue it even further and suggest that we should have available not only an instantaneous reproduction of what is happening in this place but also what is happening in committees. This would not involve a great deal of expense, technically speaking. While I am sure there are those who would cry out instantly against such a system being adopted, I think anyone who would do so has a kind of childish naivety which does not accord with the facts. 1 think it would be much better if we had the advantage of such a system when at times we are detained in our offices, and at other times when we are much more usefully employed in our offices and are not specifically involved in debates that are taking place in the house. I hope that government at an early date will make these facilities available.
I should like to comment on the remarks of the hon. member for Lotbiniere, who spoke earlier today on the regulations restricting political broadcasts. I agree with him wholeheartedly. I think we have some very foolish regulations in this respect. I do not know who wrote them, but I think they are very foolish because they seem to me to desire to make political broadcasts dull. If you have seen the number of people who normally listen to or watch political broadcasts such as "The Nation's Business", you know that they achieve the desired result, because these programs have one of the smallest listening audiences, not because the subject matter is all that boring or uninteresting but because the regulations controlling their format make it that way.
I could give a small example pointing out the ludicrousness of this situation. During the last federal election campaign, when I was a candidate, we made a number of film clips of myself touring the constituency, and what-have-you. We intended to use these film clips on various television programs. It was decided that we would add light background music to the film clips to improve the production, not necessarily of the candidate but to add some qualities to the production.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Perhaps that was needed.

I may say that it was not necessary in this case. We found that because of these regulations it was impossible to play recorded music behind the film clips. I found this baffling to the nth degree; yet it
May 30, 1967

Supply-Secretary of State was defended as being part of the regulations. If we set ourselves up as making effective political programming, nothing could be further from the truth.
In the few minutes remaining to me, Mr. Chairman-and I told the minister earlier that I was not going to take too long-I should like to take perhaps two or three more minutes to deal with an area that concerns me greatly and has for some time. That is the question of broadcasting itself. The minister told us today that appointments will be made shortly to the upper echelons of the C.B.C. This has been greeted in general, I think, as being a necessary fact and a necessary act, but I am not totally convinced of the soundness of this move. I believe it is necessary to act with all reasonable haste to alleviate many of the serious problems that exist in the C.B.C. at the moment. I think the work of the broadcasting committee, and the legislation which is proposed to bring before us shortly, will attempt to solve many of these problems. However, I would think that the danger involved in this suggestion is the same kind of danger that we have faced in our experiences over the last few months, namely that by executive action the government of the day shall usurp the powers and responsibilities of this place.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
If my guesswork is correct, the legislation that will be introduced in this house will be radically changed with regard to the responsibilities and even the method of appointment of the top officers in the C.B.C. In effect, what the government will do by making appointments now is to destroy the meaning of a good deal of the machinery that will be instituted at a later date this year. I think it would be either irresponsible of the government, or unwise of those people who are to be selected for these positions, if such a move were made. This may not be in accordance with the views of some hon. members, even on this side of the house, but I see great danger at the moment in appointing people, which would have to be done, to almost fictitious posts, because no such posts exist until the new legislation establishes them. Perhaps the minister can assuage my fears in this regard, but I am not happy with her announcement as it presently stands.
Second, we are being asked to grant a greatly increased appropriation this year for what the minister has described as a normal increase in salaries because of a threatened

strike, because of a good deal of new equipment, much of it related to colour I would imagine, and for the amortization of some of the capital products. If basically that is the purpose for which this extra money is being provided, this is indeed disturbing because it became apparent to those of us who sat on the broadcasting committee that one of the root problems of the C.B.C. was the fact that it was being strangled by having its television operation being made dependant on advertising. The way in which the problem was dealt with in the white paper did not offer a very good solution. I am not sure that the legislation will introduce a good solution, but unless we are willing to give priorities in the right order, some very fundamental ills in the C.B.C., particularly as they relate to television, will not be solved.
If we are going to make the C.B.C. into an effective instrument of public programming and broadcasting in this country, the amount of advertising revenue available must be a secondary concern. We must ask ourselves the primary question first, namely, how much Canadian content do we want in our broadcasting, what should be its quality and what will it cost us? When we have made those decisions, then I think we can turn to the question of how much we might recoup through the use of intelligent advertising, instead of setting in the beginning some kind of artificial formula or figure.
I think also, as the hon. member for Royal has suggested, we must stimulate and encourage the C.B.C. to do a great deal more in the area of public affairs. I for one have been amazed, even flabbergasted, at the amount of good and competent public affairs programming which has been done this year by the C.T.V. network even though, to my knowledge, it has not received one cent of public money to do so. I know they have done this in order to fulfil the requirements and expectations of the Board of Broadcast Governors; but if the C.T.V. network can do some of the programs of quality that I have seen, without any public money, then the C.B.C. could be encouraged to do a great deal more and better public affairs programming in the future, not programming that will either be sloughed off on limited networks, as has been the case with some of the better programing this year, or be given what might be called very poor time.
Public affairs programming by its very nature should be available to the widest audience possible, and when programs are treated in a cavalier fashion and shown either late at night or some time during the day when there
May 30. 1967

is only a small audience, this does not serve the Canadian people well.
Last year when we discussed the question of public affairs and when we dealt with the estimates for the maintenance of public archives I was concerned about the fact that the C.B.C. for some years now has been producing a great deal of quality material which, after its initial showing, is no longer available to the Canadian people. It seems to me there should be a more creative use of the thousands of feet of good film that is presently either lost or locked away in some dark cupboard somewhere. Years ago we established the National Film Board, with regional depots, for a lending film service. It seems to me that if some co-ordination could be established, much good C.B.C. footage could be made available for private showings, for discussion groups and for all kinds of local education through the National Film Board offices. I am also disturbed at the fact that a great deal of good footage has been seemingly lost or mislaid through inadequate archive facilities, both at the C.B.C. and at other archival institutions.
I should like to say a few words about a couple of very parochial issues. First of all I will refer to the problem of the national news. It seems that most of us in eastern Canada are reduced to getting an hour less of sleep per night as long as the national newscast is televised at 12 midnight rather than 11 p.m., which is generally the case in central Canada. I am reminded that in Newfoundland the news is broadcast at 12.30 a.m. I do not think it is fair to deprive a good portion of the Canadian people of an hour's sleep at night. We all need our sleep these days because of the many problems we face. I heard that this matter has been considered, but this has not been done forcefully enough because I believe that the technical problems are not all that great. I would hope that one of the good announcements the C.B.C. would make for this fall is that the national news will be made available to eastern Canada at eleven o'clock.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: That would be broadcast at five or six o'clock in British Columbia.

speechtext:
There is an earlier newscast which of course is not available to much of eastern Canada, simply because it is not carried on C.B.C. affiliates.
Finally, I should like to discuss the matter of the second service. Apparently we have been given the green light to consider the
Supply-Secretary of State possibility of a second service all across this country, and I hope that this also will be given a good deal of encouragement. I think there is reason to believe that at present there is a possibility, without hurting the public broadcasting system, of making available a second service in all parts of this country which are presently being serviced by television. I know that in my own area there is considerable concern in this regard, because of the early allocation of channels, but this is a technical problem which basically can be overcome. I would urge the minister to pursue with greater expediency the matter of the second service and the opportunities it would afford to the maritime region. In some places indeed there is not so much concern now about a second service because they are seeking a third service and, in some very fortunate areas, a fourth. I think greater attention should be given to the establishment of at least two services across the country in a day and age when it is technically possible.
In closing let me say again that I think the minister has attempted, through a very complex series of responsibilities, to be effective in administering her portfolio, and I should like to commend her in particular for the way in which she has handled effectively the kind of communications that have taken place between this house and the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I should like to go on record as supporting what the hon. member for Royal said this afternoon, that it would be a terrible thing if we ever got involved in this place in debating details of program policy. I think our job is to outline the principles on which a public broadcasting system should operate, and we should get involved as little as possible in the day to day operations of this important national service.

I think all of us, perhaps particularly those who are concerned about the future of Quebec and its relationship with the country, should be concerned with the French speaking minority that have maintained their identity through these hundreds of years in parts of the country which have not yet received equal recognition.
