Mr. Chairman, I am in the
habit of writing to the minister to give her my views on policy on occasion, and to bring to her attention any matters of direct concern to my constituents. Therefore I will not deal with any of these matters this evening.
I listened with great interest to the speech of the charming member for Prince. I agree with a considerable amount of what he said, but when he suggested that we should have television installed in our offices so that we could sit in our offices and watch the proceedings in this house, and witness the proceedings in parliamentary committees, I must say he is too much of a swinger for this old fashioned socialist.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, if I may rise on a point of privilege to clarify what I said, I did not think I went as far as suggesting television in our offices. I do not think I am yet that much of a swinger, and I doubt whether that would be necessary. Basically I was talking about some type of radio connection, some electronic connection both with this house and with committees. I think that would be a good deal less expensive and just as suitable for the use I had in mind.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: We would not have to look at you then, Bert-just listen to you.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
The hon. member would not have that experience, except possibly when I was in this house.
Anyway, Mr. Chairman, there are two reasons I object to this proposal. First of all, there is the cost involved. Second, do you think that members would come down to the house to listen to debates if they could turn on a radio and listen to what is going on from their offices, or listen in to committees? Personally I think that this is a very impractical suggestion, though I realize it was put forward in the best spirit and with the best of


intentions. I think that when the hon. member has been here a few more years he will have mellowed in that respect, and realize that this house cannot function unless there is a physical presence here.
I just want to congratulate the minister for her detailed attention to any matters that I have brought to her notice with respect to policy and matters that concern my constituency. I must say I like writing letters to the minister because I always get such a delightful reply.
I also appreciate the work of her immediate office staff and also the work of her parliamentary secretary, who 1 think pays strict attention to his job. I notice that when it comes to ten o'clock he is always here to deal with any questions concerning the minister's department, if she is not able to be present.
May I also compliment the minister on her work in connection with our centenary. From correspondence and conversations I have had with visitors to this house, from visiting Expo and other events in Canada, I have had nothing but compliments as far as the minister is concerned. She seems to be the ideal centennial leader in this country at this time. I am not saying that to be facetious; I have heard this said over and over again and I think it is only fair to repeat it here.
I also want to express my appreciation for the work being done by the centennial commission. This is a job that requires teamwork from top to bottom, whether it is work connected with Expo or with activities throughout the country. I am very pleased to say that as far as I am concerned I think this work has been very successful to date. I wish all those connected with our centennial celebrations in this country, whether at the top, the provincial or municipal level, every success in everything they undertake till this year is ended.
As far as the C.B.C. is concerned, Mr. Chairman, as I have said I usually bring my complaints to the minister in writing. However, I want to say how much I appreciate the courtesy of the officials of the C.B.C., and also Mr. Warner's services, who answers inquiries from members of parliament, obtains scripts, and things of that sort. I have found him most helpful indeed.
For years I have suggested that it would be a good policy for the C.B.C. whenever it faces an engineering problem to let its senior officials and engineers visit regions which
May 30, 1967	COMMONS
have other problems related to television, radio, and so on, meet the people in the area and inform them about what the policy of the C.B.C. is and what they are trying to accomplish in the particular area concerned.
Quite recently a Dr. Caple from Vancouver went to the Trail area to discuss with the people there the circumstances relating to television, low-power relay stations, and things of that sort, which they appreciated very much. I suggest that this policy should be continued and extended. There is nothing like getting the participation of the people at the local level, Mr. Chairman, particularly with respect to the activities of the federal government. I have made the same suggestion to other departments, and I have found that wherever any department of government is willing, shall I say, to consult the local people about any problem and to invite suggestions, the services provided to that community benefit as a result.
I should also like to say how much I appreciate the services of Dr. Lamb and his staff in the archives, which I sometimes have occasion to visit. I am very interested in history, particularly the history of my own region, and I do appreciate the co-operation that I have received from this gentleman and also the lady staff. I noticed recently with considerable pleasure that the "Lamb" in the archives became a lion when it came to the act to establish a corporation for the administration of the National Museums of Canada, and I can well understand it. I think that before our museums are administered by a corporation as suggested in this bill, this matter will require further consideration.
I am not going to say anything about the National Museum at this time; I will save my remarks until we are discussing the bill that is on the order paper, which deals with the establishment of a corporation for the administration of the National Museum of Canada. I want to make some comments at that time about the organization of staff for the museum. All I can say at the moment is that I hope something will be done in the very near future to commence the construction of the building that is so necessary to house the National Museum and the work that is undertaken by its staff.
I have had, Mr. Chairman, a few complaints about the purchase of pictures by the Canada Council. I find these complaints usually come from middle aged ladies who were brought up at the same time as I was 27053-49!

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
I wish to join those who have extended congratulations to the minister and to the department for which she is responsible. I congratulate her for the great events taking place in this country to mark our one hundredth birthday of confederation.
The centennial commission is working wonders for Canadianism; it is doing a tremendous job in Canada. That we may all concede. It gives me great pleasure to congratulate the minister for such exciting undertakings as the centennial pageants of all kinds including the train, caravans, canoe races and Expo as well as all those other exercises and pageants, great and small, in this country.
I said some time ago in this chamber and made the same point in a recent news letter that I distributed in my constituency that in my view the events taking place in connection with the centenary of confederation celebrations are making Canada the most exciting and dynamic country in the western world. I repeat that here, unequivocally. Every day, as I see young people and the not so young in my constituency and elsewhere, I am reminded of the importance and the impact of these confederation events and of the impact they are having on the souls of Canadians, regardless of their ethnic and racial backgrounds
In talking, however, on the estimates of the Department of the Secretary of State and particularly the estimates of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation my remarks will not be so laudatory or pleasant. I did not exactly come to bury Caesar; but neither did I come to praise him. At this juncture I cannot join in the paean of praise, though I see signs that C.B.C. programs have improved. I wish to second something the hon. member for Prince mentioned, when speaking on the subject. He anticipated what I was going to say and said it more eloquently than I could have said it. He referred to the estimates for the C.B.C. this year being increased by an amount of $29.5 million to a total of something like $143.5 million-with little or no explanation of where the money is going. Tonight, tomorrow, the next day and the next day-until an answer is given-millions of Canadian taxpayers will be asking where that $143 million for the C.B.C. is going.
With costs and taxes at their present levels, with the average wage earner and taxpayer

caught in the squeeze in which he is caught, I do not think we can afford to spend $143 million this year on the C.B.C.
Certainly, the Canadian taxpayer cannot afford to have that amount spent, sight unseen, without knowing where it is going.
I suggest that the crucial aspect of passing these estimates lies ahead of us. It is not enough to place an item in the estimates and expect passage in this chamber without questions being asked. Questions will be asked and I doubt if the estimates, or this particular item, will pass until they are answered to the satisfaction of many hon. members and the people at home whom we represent.
I think the C.B.C. has done and continues to do constructive work in the field of English and French relations in Canada-in other words, in the field of Canadian unity. I salute the efforts that the corporation has made under the wise counsel and leadership of its distinguished president in this direction. The efforts are mighty and many. It strikes me, though, that much as the corporation is obviously interested in improving Canadian unity and in improving relations between the peoples and communities that make Canada a nation, it is not interested and in fact is inclined to be distinterested in bringing together the communities on the North American continent-and here I speak of the great community of the United States and our community of Canada. If, in fact, many public affairs programs of the C.B.C. are not actually divisive-that is, if they do not actually tend to divide Canada and the United States-there at least is no effort in many of these programs to improve understanding between our communities. There is no effort to enhance and enlarge social and intellectual intercourse between these great societies and to bring about greater understanding between us.
Without exaggerating, it can be said that many C.B.C. public affairs programs seem to labour under the delusion that to establish our Canadian manhood we must be antiUnited States. The corporation thinks that we must talk and sound as if we in this country do not like the United States. I do not subscribe to that school, Mr. Chairman. I am pro-Canadian, but I am pro-United States also, and I am pro-English and pro-French. I believe that many of the less responsible public affairs programs put out by the C.B.C. in the past two years have in them the seeds of potential harm, and may well destroy friendly Canadian and United States relations. The
May 30, 1967	COMMONS
philosophy behind such programs may be the result of omission rather than commission. But if it is a deliberate philosophy, it is a puny one, sir. It is a philosophy which is unbecoming to the C.B.C. or to Canada or to any part of this great nation.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
I do not believe the United States is any more correct in many of the things it does than are any other of the societies on the face of this earth. At the same time, the fact is that we in North America live with, toil with and work for a better world alongside the people of the United States in a far greater measure of involvement than any other society. Perhaps our two societies are intermingled and involved in this manner to a far greater degree than are any other two societies on the face of the earth. It is unrealistic at best, and destructive at worst, to foster a cult of dislike, disharmony, discredit and unfounded enmity toward that society to our south to which we are so closely related in blood, in economics, in philosophy, in origin and in the goals we set ourselves.
I think the C.B.C. probably has a greater responsibility than almost any other broadcasting network in the world in terms of its influence upon public opinion. I doubt whether this statement is much of an exaggeration if, indeed, it is an exaggeration at all. There are few societies I can think of, looking back on my experience as a journalist and a broadcaster before I came to this house, which have as great a susceptibility to one medium of communication as the Canadian society has to the C.B.C. media. Because of the disparate nature of our social situation in Canada, because of the great distances which separate us, because of the geographic divisions which are intensified by differing economic ambitions, because of regional, racial and ethnic differences, because of religious differences, because of the degree to which our population is spread out along one thin line across 3,500 miles of territory, and then sparsely dotted across the rest of a country which covers almost four billion square miles, the C.B.C., supported by public funds and having the prestige which comes from its title, its history, its good fortune in being first on the scene, and through some of the excellent work it has done during the last quarter of a century, has an impact on Canadian society which probably is unrivalled by any other broadcasting network in any other country in the world.
This being so, it behooves the executives of the corporation, particularly those who are responsible for programming, and for public
DEBATES	769
Supply-Secretary of State affairs programming in particular, to exercise extreme caution and the most extreme conscientiousness and responsibility in the area of program pronouncements, directions and themes. I wonder whether some of those with authority over public affairs programming at the C.B.C. understand this awesome responsibility and, if they do, whether they recharge themselves every day to live up to it properly.
The hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke spoke this afternoon with some eloquence on the power of television. He gave us a profound description of the impact of television, one with which I agree totally. I do not altogether agree with the essence of his argument in connection with the televising of important international and public events, but that is irrelevant to the point I am making at the moment. I do agree 100 per cent with what I have called his profound description of the impact of television.
The hon. member was asked to give his assessment of the impact of print journalism as compared with television. He answered, correctly I believe, to the effect that there was really no comparison in terms of immediate impact and influence between electronic journalism and print journalism. I have never been able to agree with the old dictum that a picture is worth a thousand words, because it is too general a statement. Certainly no picture is worth a Shakespeare sonnet. No picture is worth the Gettysburg address. No picture is worth certain songs or scriptural texts that a lot of us can think of. But a picture, depending on the angle at which it is shot, can certainly distort a thousand words. In this sense a picture can be worth, or unworthy of, a thousand words or even a million words.
This is the danger attaching to electronic pictorial journalism. Television journalists must be studiously and conscientiously aware at all times of the danger of distortion, of imbalance, which can arise from misuse of the potent, awesome weapon which they hold in their hands as their journalistic tool, one which few if any of us understand at this point in the development of our society and electronic technology.
What is crucial about electronic journalism is the editing; and the question which counts is: What winds up on the cutting floor? The question which expresses our concern for the journalistic welfare of the society in which we live, both nationally and internationally, is: What is edited out of a television news story? The hon. member for Burin-Burgeo making his maiden speech in this house two or three weeks ago spoke just as eloquently
May 30, 19B7

Supply-Secretary of State as did the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke today, except that he took a somewhat different line, when he described to members of this chamber the immense and as yet uncomprehended power of television. There were many frightening suggestions and implications in his remarks, which gave all of us cause to stop and ponder the direction in which we are moving in terms of electronic journalism. He stressed the tremendous impact and influence of the medium, and, more important still, he pointed out that we do not yet understand how to handle it properly.
I have had some stern things to say about electronic journalism as far as the C.B.C. is concerned, particularly in the field of public affairs programming. Since returning from Viet Nam and other parts of southeast Asia a few weeks ago I have spoken publicly in the Winnipeg area on the subject of the agonizing war there and its coverage. I have criticized the C.B.C., among others, for what I feel has been an imbalanced reporting job. Understandably, I have elicited some reaction, a good deal of which has been highly vocal. Some of my critics, some of those who feel I have spoken unreasonably and perhaps irresponsibly, have suggested that it is unfair to criticize C.B.C. television for shortcomings of this nature since C.B.C. television is doing such a tremendous job in the field of school broadcasts and educational programming. I concede the point, but as an argument it does not wash.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
What these people fail to realize, or at least to concede, is that all television is educational. All television is educational television. Some of it is good education, and some of it is frightfully poor education. What I have asked for in the public pronouncements I have made on this subject is balance in C.B.C. public affairs programming. I am not a part owner of any newspaper, so I have no particular justification for criticizing the jobs that certain newspapers may do in the reporting field; but I am a part owner of the C.B.C, as is everybody in this chamber, everybody in the galleries, and everybody across the country and because of that we have at least the right to demand excellence and balance in public affairs reporting.
A few months ago there was considerable controversy over the interview conducted by C.B.C. one Sunday night with Mr. von Thadden of the Republic of Germany. There was much controversy over whether the interview should be broadcast by the C.B.C.,

and indeed over whether he should be allowed into the country. I believe the controversy should have started after the interview, not before it. The interview did more harm than good because of the manner in which it was conducted. It was frightfully badly handled. As a news interview it bordered on the destructive.
The people who handled the interview for the C.B.C approached it as they would have approached an interview with Miss America. What people in the C.B.C. and all other electronic journalistic media must remember, when they are talking to persons who are forming and helping create public opinion throughout the world, helping to shape public affairs at any level and in any nation, is that this is the big league. They are dealing with people who are highly qualified, cunning, and at least as intelligent as those who are conducting the interviews, if not far more intelligent.
When dealing with a subject as explosive and dangerous as the von Thadden interview, the interviewer should be ready for his subject. I would have no objection to having an interview with Adolf Hitler on C.B.C. television if it were handled properly and the interviewer were properly prepared; but the von Thadden interview was badly handled and left people with an entirely wrong impression, not only of the man but of the force of the issue with which they were concerned in that particular television episode. I thought it was distinctly bad journalism.
I think my views are shared by a great many Canadians when I speak of the imbalance, of the inequality, of the naivety and of the ill-preparedness of a good many of the C.B.C public affairs programs. I had considerable mail and comment on the subject from people in all parts of Canada after I got back from the Far East and made my first statements on the subject of Viet Nam. Lest people think I am alone in this matter, I will remind hon. members that the hon. member for Leeds made a very well documented and far-reaching speech on this subject in Winnipeg on December 8,	1966. He addressed the
Canadian Club in Winnipeg on the very subject which I am discussing, and pointed out the imbalance and the inequality in the C.B.C.'s approach to political issues of the day in this country and throughout the world. I do not intend to quote from his speech; most members of the committee are probably familiar with the address he delivered. It was one of the best received and most thoroughly documented pronouncements on this subject that
May 30. 1967

to my knowledge has been made in the history of television in Canada.
In any event, he, I and others feel it necessary to speak out on this issue, not just for ourselves but for thousands of Canadians who also feel concerned and who would like to speak if they had the opportunity. A few moments ago I mentioned Viet Nam, that agonizing war and the news coverage of it. I do not know who is right in Viet Nam or who is wrong, no more than does anybody in this chamber, or for that matter anybody in the world. It is an agony for all of us, and all of us devoutly wish it could be ended tonight.
However, when I say I do not know who is right I still reserve the right to form my opinions on the basis of balanced and objective reporting, and I do not want to be brainwashed into a particular point of view by the C.B.C. Although I may not know who is right on that issue I do know that the C.B.C is not right on it, and that from March, 1965 to March, 1967 by its approach to the Viet Nam issue and American involvement in Viet Nam it has generated much more heat than light.
It was this issue more than any other that really led me to the conclusion that there has been a serious imbalance in C.B.C. public affairs programming that has led to an anti-Americanism which has not escaped everybody's notice. The question of censorship by omission is the question that arises in an issue such as this one. It is not so much what is done as what is not done.
In connection with the Viet Nam war a number of questions have been covered quite thoroughly by the C.B.C., but a number of others have been ignored altogether. The C.B.C., for examples, has given a lot of coverage to the trend on the part of some young Americans to come to Canada to escape the United States draft and the war. I do not care to take a stand on that question. It is a newsworthy item and deserves some of the documentary attention it has received. But on the basis of the best figures I have been able to get from the United States defence department and Canadian immigration authorities, the ratio between young Canadians going to the United States to enlist in the marines and fight in Viet Nam and young Americans coming to Canada to escape the draft is nine to one.
Some 2,700 Canadians have enlisted in the United States marines to fight in Viet Nam. Approximately 300 American youths have come to Canada to escape the draft. I do not wish to argue which is right, but if we are paying $143 million to the C.B.C., of which all
Supply-Secretary of State of us own a part, and when we consider that in many communities the C.B.C. is the only source of major news, we have a right to ask for balanced reporting on an issue such as this. This evening I should like to make some remarks about the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, although 1 intend to reserve most of them until we reach a consideration of specific items. Let me say that I think it unfortunate that some members seem to view the C.B.C. as a variety of the sacred cow. They take exception to any member of the house who offers any criticism. I have criticized the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in the past and I intend to do so again in the future. I hope my criticism will be constructive.
There is only one aspect of the C.B.C. I criticize. I am thoroughly in favour of and endorse approximately three quarters of its operations. I believe here in the house is the proper place to bring forward proper criticism, either one's own or that which has been provided by constituents or other individuals throughout the country. I think this is particularly true when the criticism is directed toward policy or the lack of it. Having made those remarks I shall reserve most of my comments about the C.B.C. until later.
It has been fashionable here and elsewhere to believe that one should never present a case on behalf of someone who allegedly has been mistreated unless that person is without the ability or facilities to defend himself or herself, as the case may be. When one presents such a case in this house the press and others naturally have some sympathy and look into the matter. If an individual happens to be of importance or prominence we generally consider he is able to fend for himself, and very seldom does a member bring such a case before this assembly.
This afternoon the hon. member for York-Humber brought such a case to the attention of his house, and I refer to his remarks in reference to Lord Thomson. I realize that Lord Thomson with his string of newspa pers is able to look after himself. That is not the particular aspect of the case which concerns me, but rather the principle. I am particularly anxious to put my remarks on the record this evening so the Secretary of State will have an opportunity to consult the law officers and give an answer tomorrow, or at some time when her estimates are being considered.
The facts surrounding the loss of Lord Thomson's Canadian citizenship have been placed before this house during the question
May 30, 1967

period and on other occasions. The government has always sloughed them off by refusing to provide an answer. Surely we should have a proper explanation from the Secretary of State on this occasion. This is a very serious matter in that a native born Canadian has been deprived of his citizenship for no other reason than that he accepted some sort of honour from another country. It is very strange that an individual can spy on his own country, betray his own country or commit murder without losing his citizenship, yet if he accepts an honorary degree or some sort of title he will lose that citizenship. This is a very dangerous precedent to set and I think the government should make very clear what is intended in this regard.

Winnipeg North Centre said, he lost his premiership; but I do not think it was for that reason. I think this matter should be clarified. What sort of title, declaration or award is included in this policy, and in what instances does one lose citizenship for accepting these titles?
Lord Thomson was used as an example by the hon. member for York-Humber. Let us suppose Lord Thomson had accepted a title or an honorary degree from, say, the King of Sweden. I presume that Lord Thomson would in that case be stateless. Where would he go? These are questions that I think should be answered. If it is all right to accept honourary degrees or orders from monarchs such as the King of Greece-and the case of the former premier of Quebec is an example-why is it an offence to accept them from our own Queen Elizabeth? It seems very peculiar to me, and I hope the Secretary of State can explain these things. They have never been explained to date.
When this resolution-I believe it was brought forward in the form of a resolution many years ago-was drafted I should like to know whether the opinion of the law officers of the crown was sought as to whether it was valid. Since then the citizenship act has been 27053-50

Supply-Secretary of State passed. I recall-I am again speaking from memory at the moment-that there was a provision that any British subject domiciled in Canada shall not accept a title. I believe this was before the present citizenship act was passed.
I thnk this matter should be clarified so I again ask, why has Lord Thomson lost his Canadian citizenship? Is there any other reason for this? Is there any statute, order in council or anything of that nature which provides that a native born Canadian can lose his or her citizenship for accepting a foreign title? If so, I think the government should give very serious consideration to rectifying the situation. Here we have the case of a prominent man who has contributed much to Canada and has lost his citizenship for accepting a minor honour, because it really is a minor honour, from our own Queen.
This seems a very peculiar state of affairs and I think it should be clarified. In any event, Mr. Chairman, I do not know why the government should be particularly concerned with these matters. All sorts of people receive medals and orders which are really exactly the same as titles, and which I understand in many cases entitle them to be called certain things. They receive them from His Holiness, for example.
I think it is fine to receive these honours and I do not know why the government has to stick its nose in, so to speak, and concern itself with the official recognition. If a Canadian citizen should for meritorious service in some field receive an award from another country, I do not understand why it is not possible for that citizen to receive the honour and retain citizenship in this country.
There is no reason why the government should recognize these honours or titles. In the Republic of France I believe that people call themselves dukes, counts and so on, and they are described as such in the social columns. I do not believe the government of France recognizes them as such. I do not think our government should start passing out titles-I have put myself on record before in this regard-but I am glad to see that we are now granting recognition for service to Canada. But if other countries give decorations or make awards to Canadian citizens, I do not understand why those citizens should not be able to accept the honours and retain Canadian citizenship. This is none of the government's business.
I see no reason why a native born Canadian citizen should be deprived of his citizenship

I do not expect the Secretary of State to answer this evening, because a rather technical matter is involved here, but I hope she will answer before her estimates are passed.

LABOUR RELATIONS-CONFEDERATION OF NATIONAL TRADE UNIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Friday, militants of the Confederation of National Trade Unions by the hundreds organized public demonstrations in about 15 communities of the province of Quebec against the labour policy of the central government in Ottawa which, by 27053-50J
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion refusing to recognize natural negotiation units is infringing directly upon freedom of association.
These protests occurred in front of federal buildings in Sherbrooke, Asbestos, Magog, Windsor, Thetford Mines, Drummondville, Victoriaville, St. Johns, Beauharnois, Hull, Chicoutimi, Alma and in front of the C.B.C. buildings in Montreal and in Quebec city. Unless this dispute is settled immediately, it is to be expected that other demonstrations of this type will occur as well as a march on parliament by thousands of Quebec workers.
The government cannot plead ignorance of the facts, as the grievances raised by the C.N.T.U. have been well known for the last year and a half and as it has been promising a decision for more than thirteen months. But the systematic standpatism of the Pearson government is an illustration of its indecision and pusillanimity-

maintopic: LABOUR RELATIONS-CONFEDERATION OF NATIONAL TRADE UNIONS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: LABOUR RELATIONS-CONFEDERATION OF NATIONAL TRADE UNIONS
speechtext:
-which now border on dishonesty, in spite of the laughter of Quebec Liberal members, and which could seriously aggravate a conflict which has already gone too far.
The Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Marchand), as a former president of the C.N.T.U., caused a great disappointment to his former fellow workers when he proved inefficient in this regard in the cabinet and when he refused to recognize special considerations to Quebec, in all fields. The 200,000 members of the C.N.T.U. who paid him a good salary for so many years are under the strong impression that he has disowned their sacred interests to satisfy his own personal ambitions, thus supporting centralizing policies and uniform administrative standards throughout Canada.
In summary, what do thousands and thousands of Quebec workers demand? They simply want to choose their own trade union, and they refuse to be imposed upon by trade-union structures unilaterally established by the employer or its agencies, and even subjected to foreign influence. In short, it is the whole question of labour freedom which is involved, as well as some particular views of the Quebec workers who, on account of their different culture, have special needs which do not always agree with those of the great majority of workers in the nine other provinces.

Therefore, Ottawa must amend the Industrial Relations Act and Bill No. C-170 to allow natural negotiation units. In addition, the president of the Canadian Labour Relations Board must be bilingual and the principle of parity labour representation must be recognized, as well as the right to vote for the president of the C.L.R.B. in case of conflict between labour unions.
Mr. Speaker, those are rightful demands based on freedom, justice and equality. I have spoken more than ten times in this house in the last 13 months. In April 1966, the cabinet set up a special committee to study those requests. Every federal member of parliament from Quebec was questioned and the great majority of them came out publicly in favour of the C.N.T.U.'s suggestions, as can be seen from the booklet entitled Parole de depute. And I find on page 16 of that booklet that the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Mackasey), who is getting ready to answer on behalf of the minister, agreed with the four requests of the C.N.T.U. I hope that tonight he will not disappoint that labour union.
The representatives of the C.N.T.U. came here to parliament to discuss those problems with the ministers and members. They will come back for the last time next Thursday to meet the ministers.
It is more than ever time to solve those problems before the dissatisfaction of the people reaches alarming and extensive proportions. The government should not forget the recent march of 25,000 farmers on parliament; it should get out of its ivory tower and legislate for the rights of the people and not for an undemocratic bureaucracy and sometimes unions too subserviently ruled by cosmopolitan and foreign interests.

When the hon. member for Sherbrooke stated that I agreed with many aspects of the brief of the C.N.T.U. concerning their particular problems, he is accurate. I personally feel that this particular problem has dragged too long. It has been well over a year since a special committee of the cabinet was established to solve the particular problem of whether or not the

C.N.T.U. has a legitimate grievance with reference to the definition of a bargaining unit.
I do agree, too, with the representations of the hon. member for Sherbrooke on the question of increased bilingualism. I am very pleased that every effort is now being made when different groups appear before the Labour Relations Board to make certain they are under no handicap, regardless of which official language they choose to use before that board. The very latest in simultaneous translation equipment is placed at the disposal of each and every person participating in these particular proceedings.
I should like however to limit my remarks at this moment because of one particular reason the hon. member has pointed out. I refer to the fact that representatives of the C.N.T.U. will meet with representatives of the cabinet here on Thursday. Anything that I may say now could be misconstrued and could build up false hopes, or dash the hopes of the very people who are coming here to meet with the cabinet committee. I do agree with the hon. member for Sherbrooke that almost 13 months have elapsed since the cabinet committee was struck, and the time has now arrived to make a decision.
